Leveled is the right default for general-purpose KV workloads where you have updates and need predictable read latency. For your workload — append-only, time-prefixed, write-bound — the trade-offs flip.

## Write amplification: the headline difference

Leveled compaction's invariant is that each level is roughly 10x larger than the last (the level multiplier). To maintain it, every key gets rewritten ~once per level it traverses. Six levels = 6x rewrite minimum, often 10x-30x in practice with overlap and partial compaction.

Universal compaction merges files in size tiers. A new file lands at the top, and when N files of similar size accumulate they merge into one larger file. Total rewrites per key are roughly `log_N(total_size / memtable_size)` — typically 3-5 rewrites for terabyte-scale data with N=4.

For 50k writes/sec sustained over 90 days:
- Leveled: ~1.3 PB written to disk (assuming 1 KB events, 30x write amp).
- Universal: ~200 TB written. Same data ingested.

That's a 6x difference in disk write bandwidth and SSD wear. On NVMe with 3 GB/s sustained writes, leveled at this rate is borderline; universal has comfortable headroom.

## The L0 stall problem

Leveled's failure mode at high sustained write rates: L0 files can overlap each other (they're not range-partitioned), so the L0 -> L1 compaction must consider all overlapping L0 files. If writes outpace L0 -> L1, L0 files accumulate. RocksDB defaults:

```
level0_slowdown_writes_trigger = 20
level0_stop_writes_trigger = 36
```

At 20 L0 files, RocksDB throttles writers. At 36, it stops them. At 50k writes/sec your memtable flushes 1-2 SSTs per second. If L0 -> L1 compaction runs once per few seconds, you have minutes before stalls.

Universal doesn't have this problem because there's no L0/L1 distinction — files just merge in tiers as they accumulate.

## Space amplification: where universal usually loses, but doesn't here

Universal's worst case is 2x: during a major compaction of the largest tier you temporarily have the input and output on disk. With overwrites/deletes scattered through your data, that 2x is real.

For append-only time-series, the universe of unique keys keeps growing — there are no overwrites to GC. The 2x worst case becomes ~1.2x because compactions are mostly merging non-overlapping key ranges (different time windows).

## TTL interacts well with universal

For 90-day retention:

```cpp
rocksdb::Options options;
rocksdb::ColumnFamilyOptions cf_opts;
cf_opts.compaction_style = rocksdb::kCompactionStyleUniversal;
cf_opts.ttl = 90 * 24 * 60 * 60;  // 90 days in seconds
```

RocksDB will drop entire SST files whose youngest key is older than TTL during compaction. Universal's larger files mean fewer files to evaluate, and bulk-drop is efficient.

Better pattern for hard time bounds: **column family per day** (or per week). Drop the column family wholesale at 90 days. No compaction filter overhead, instant deletion, no fragmentation.

## Where leveled would still win

- If you started doing point lookups and tail latency mattered. Leveled gives 1 SST per level (`max_files_per_level` enforced); universal can have N files at the top tier, so a point lookup may probe more SSTs.
- If your data is highly compressible and space amp directly costs money.

## The merge itself

RocksDB doesn't iterate across CFs natively. You open one iterator per CF and merge in application code:

```cpp
std::vector<rocksdb::ColumnFamilyHandle*> handles = day_handles_in_range(t0, t1);
std::vector<rocksdb::Iterator*> iters;
db->NewIterators(read_opts, handles, &iters);
for (auto* it : iters) it->Seek(start_key);

// Min-heap by key
auto cmp = [](Iterator* a, Iterator* b) {
  return a->key().compare(b->key()) > 0;
};
std::priority_queue<Iterator*, std::vector<Iterator*>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);
for (auto* it : iters) if (it->Valid()) pq.push(it);

while (!pq.empty()) {
  Iterator* top = pq.top(); pq.pop();
  emit(top->key(), top->value());
  top->Next();
  if (top->Valid() && top->key().compare(end_key) <= 0) pq.push(top);
}
```

For a 7-day scan that's a 7-way heap merge. Per emitted record: one heap pop, one Next() on an iterator, one heap push. That's ~50 ns of overhead on top of the actual SST read. Compared to the network and serialization cost of streaming results to a client, it's invisible.

## Why it's usually fine

For 90-day retention with daily CFs, your scans land in one of these buckets:

- "Last hour" / "today" — 1 CF, no merge.
- "Last 24 hours" — 1-2 CFs.
- "Last week" — 7 CFs. 7-way heap merge is trivial.
- "Last 30 days" — 30 CFs. Now you're feeling it; the merge is still O(log 30) per record, ~5x more comparisons, but the dominant cost is reading the data.

The pathological case is cross-everything analytics. Don't do those on the live store; replicate to ClickHouse or Parquet for that.

## The hybrid: weekly CFs

Daily CFs are simple but excessive. Weekly CFs over 90 days: 13 CFs. Almost every query touches 1-2 CFs. Wholesale drops happen weekly instead of daily — fine for retention precision.

Monthly CFs (4 of them) is even less merging but means you keep up to 30 days of "about to be deleted" data. Trade off granularity for simplicity.

## The escape hatch: stop building this yourself

At this point you're hand-rolling what TimescaleDB or InfluxDB does in one config option. If you're not committed to RocksDB-as-library, **TimescaleDB** is worth a serious look:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (ts timestamptz NOT NULL, payload jsonb);
SELECT create_hypertable('events', 'ts', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '1 day');
SELECT add_retention_policy('events', INTERVAL '90 days');
```

That's it. Behind the scenes:
- Automatic chunk-per-day (your CF-per-day, but transparent).
- Chunk exclusion at query time — only relevant chunks get scanned, no app-side merging.
- BRIN-or-btree per chunk for sub-day filtering.
- Optional per-chunk columnar compression after N days, often 10-20x.
- Drop-chunk for retention is the same wholesale-delete trick.
- 50k writes/sec is well within range with proper batching.

TimescaleDB on a beefy box vs RocksDB-from-scratch with daily CFs: same architecture, an order of magnitude less code you maintain.

- Embedded service, must avoid an external DB, comfortable with C++ ops: **RocksDB + universal compaction + weekly CFs**. Heap-merge across CFs is fine.
- Anything else, especially "we run on Kubernetes and have a Postgres operator": **TimescaleDB**. You'll ship a year sooner.

Let me walk through this carefully, because the order-2 pole is exactly where this integral catches people.

**Step 1: Complexify.** Replace $\cos x$ by $e^{ix}$ and take the real part at the end:
$$I = \mathrm{Re} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{ix}}{(x^2+a^2)^2}\,dx.$$
The integrand is real and even, so the imaginary part already vanishes; but conceptually, $e^{ix}$ is what lets us use the upper-half-plane contour.

**Step 2: Pick the contour.** Close with a semicircle $C_R$ of radius $R$ in the **upper** half-plane. In that half-plane, $|e^{iz}| = e^{-\mathrm{Im}\,z} \le 1$ and decays as we go up. On $C_R$ the integrand is bounded by $1/(R^2-a^2)^2 \sim 1/R^4$, and the arc length is $\pi R$, so the arc integral is $O(1/R^3) \to 0$ (Jordan's lemma is overkill here; direct ML estimate suffices).

The poles of $1/(z^2+a^2)^2$ are at $z = \pm ia$, each of order 2. The contour encloses only $z = ia$.

**Step 3: Residue at a double pole.** Write
$$f(z) = \frac{e^{iz}}{(z-ia)^2 (z+ia)^2}.$$
For a pole of order 2 at $z_0$,
$$\mathrm{Res}_{z_0} f = \lim_{z\to z_0} \frac{d}{dz}\!\left[(z-z_0)^2 f(z)\right].$$
Here $(z-ia)^2 f(z) = e^{iz}/(z+ia)^2$, so
$$\mathrm{Res}_{ia} f = \frac{d}{dz}\!\left[\frac{e^{iz}}{(z+ia)^2}\right]_{z=ia}.$$
Quotient/product rule:
$$\frac{d}{dz}\frac{e^{iz}}{(z+ia)^2} = \frac{i e^{iz}(z+ia)^2 - e^{iz}\cdot 2(z+ia)}{(z+ia)^4} = \frac{e^{iz}\bigl[i(z+ia) - 2\bigr]}{(z+ia)^3}.$$
Evaluate at $z = ia$: $z+ia = 2ia$, $e^{iz} = e^{i(ia)} = e^{-a}$, and $i(z+ia)-2 = i(2ia)-2 = -2a - 2$. So
$$\mathrm{Res}_{ia} f = \frac{e^{-a}(-2a-2)}{(2ia)^3} = \frac{-2(a+1)e^{-a}}{-8 i a^3} = \frac{(a+1)e^{-a}}{4 i a^3}.$$

**Step 4: Assemble.** By the residue theorem,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{ix}}{(x^2+a^2)^2}\,dx = 2\pi i \cdot \frac{(a+1)e^{-a}}{4 i a^3} = \frac{\pi (a+1) e^{-a}}{2 a^3}.$$
Taking the real part (the integral is already real),
$$\boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\cos x}{(x^2+a^2)^2}\,dx = \frac{\pi (1+a)}{2 a^3}\, e^{-a}.}$$

**Sanity checks.**
- **Dimensional:** scaling $x = a u$ shows the integral equals $a^{-3}$ times a function of $a$. Good.
- **Small $a$:** the integrand concentrates near 0, integral $\sim a^{-3}$. Our formula gives $\pi/(2a^3) + \pi/(2a^2) + \dots$, consistent.
- **Parameter-differentiation check.** The classical result $\int \cos x/(x^2+a^2)\,dx = (\pi/a)e^{-a}$ can be differentiated with respect to $a^2$: $-\partial_{a^2}$ of the integrand gives $1/(x^2+a^2)^2$, and $-\partial_{a^2}[(\pi/a) e^{-a}] = -\frac{1}{2a}\partial_a[(\pi/a)e^{-a}] = \frac{\pi(1+a)e^{-a}}{2a^3}$. Matches exactly.

**The two traps, summarized.**
1. **Only upper-half poles count** when you close upward *and* the integrand has the form $e^{iz}g(z)$ with $g$ decaying. Closing downward with $e^{iz}$ fails because $|e^{iz}|$ blows up in the lower half-plane. (If the integrand had $\cos x$ directly without complexifying, you couldn't pick a half-plane at all.)
2. **Order-2 residues need a derivative.** The formula $\mathrm{Res} = \lim (z-z_0) f(z)$ is only for simple poles. For order $n$: take $(z-z_0)^n f(z)$, differentiate $n-1$ times, divide by $(n-1)!$, then evaluate.

An iterator implements `__iter__` (returns self) and `__next__` (returns next value or raises StopIteration). But in practice, generators are usually simpler.

**Class-based iterator — chunked reader:**
```python
class ChunkedReader:
    """Read a file in fixed-size chunks."""
    def __init__(self, filepath: str, chunk_size: int = 1024):
        self.filepath = filepath
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
        self._file = None

    def __iter__(self):
        self._file = open(self.filepath, 'rb')
        return self

    def __next__(self) -> bytes:
        chunk = self._file.read(self.chunk_size)
        if not chunk:
            self._file.close()
            raise StopIteration
        return chunk

for chunk in ChunkedReader('large_file.bin', 4096):
    process(chunk)
```

**Generator equivalent (usually preferred):**
```python
def chunked_reader(filepath: str, chunk_size: int = 1024):
    with open(filepath, 'rb') as f:
        while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):
            yield chunk
```

The generator version is shorter, handles cleanup automatically via `with`, and is easier to reason about.

**When to use the class-based approach:**
- When you need to maintain complex state between iterations
- When you need `__len__` or `__contains__` on the iterator
- When you need to serialize/pickle the iterator's position
- When building a public API where the iterator is a first-class object

The key insight: each distribution models a specific **data-generating process**. Don't think "which formula?" Think "what is physically happening to produce this data?"

**Start with three questions:**

1. **Discrete or continuous?** Are you counting things (0, 1, 2, ...) or measuring things (3.7, 14.2, ...)?
2. **What are you counting/measuring?** Successes? Events? Time until something happens?
3. **What are the assumptions?** Fixed number of trials? Constant rate? Independence?

**The discrete family (counting things):**

| Distribution | You're counting... | Key assumption | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bernoulli** | Success/failure in ONE trial | Two outcomes, fixed probability p | One coin flip |
| **Binomial(n, p)** | Successes in n fixed trials | Independent trials, same p each time | 20 coin flips, count heads |
| **Geometric(p)** | Trials until FIRST success | Independent trials, same p | Flips until first head |
| **Negative Binomial(r, p)** | Trials until rth success | Independent trials, same p | Flips until 5th head |
| **Poisson(lambda)** | Events in a fixed interval | Events occur independently at constant rate | Emails per hour |
| **Hypergeometric** | Successes in n draws WITHOUT replacement | Finite population, no replacement | 5 cards from a deck, count aces |

**The continuous family (measuring things):**

| Distribution | You're measuring... | Key assumption | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Exponential(lambda)** | Time until next event | Events arrive at constant rate (Poisson process) | Time between emails |
| **Gamma(k, lambda)** | Time until kth event | Poisson process | Time until 5th email |
| **Normal(mu, sigma)** | Sum/average of many small effects | Central Limit Theorem applies | Height, test scores |
| **Uniform(a, b)** | Outcome equally likely anywhere in [a, b] | Complete ignorance / symmetry | Random number generator |
| **Beta(a, b)** | A probability or proportion | Bounded between 0 and 1 | Batting average, click-through rate |

**The critical connections:**

- Binomial → Poisson: when n is large and p is small, Binomial(n, p) ≈ Poisson(np). This is why rare events (accidents, mutations, typos) follow Poisson.
- Poisson ↔ Exponential: if events arrive as Poisson(lambda), the waiting time between events is Exponential(lambda). Two sides of the same coin.
- Geometric is the discrete analog of Exponential (both model "time until first success" but in discrete vs. continuous time).
- Binomial → Normal: when np and n(1-p) are both > 10, the binomial is approximately Normal(np, np(1-p)).
Okay this helps a lot. But here's where I get stuck — in practice, how do I tell the difference between, say, a Poisson situation and a Binomial situation? They can give similar numbers.

The numbers can look similar — that's exactly why the Poisson approximation to the binomial works. But the **underlying process** is different, and choosing wrong means your assumptions are wrong, which means your confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are wrong.

**The key question: do you know the denominator?**

- **Binomial:** You have a fixed number of trials n, and you count how many succeeded. You know both the numerator AND the denominator. "Out of 200 patients given the drug, 34 had side effects."
- **Poisson:** You count events in a window (time, area, volume), but there's no fixed number of "trials." You know the count but NOT the denominator. "There were 12 ER admissions between 8pm and midnight."

For the ER example: you can't say "out of X potential patients, 12 showed up." There's no natural X. The population that *could* have shown up is vague and huge. That's Poisson territory.

For the drug example: you know exactly 200 people took the drug. That's binomial territory.

**Another diagnostic: can the count exceed a natural maximum?**

Binomial is bounded above by n (can't have more successes than trials). Poisson is unbounded — in principle, 1000 people could show up at the ER in one hour. If your count has no natural ceiling, lean Poisson.

**A worked example**

Suppose a call center gets an average of 8 calls per hour.

*Poisson framing:* calls arrive independently at rate lambda = 8/hour. P(exactly 5 calls in an hour) = e^(-8) * 8^5 / 5! = 0.0916.

*Could you frame it as binomial?* You'd have to say: "there are n potential callers, each with probability p of calling in this hour, and np = 8." But what is n? The entire customer base? The whole city? You don't know n, and the answer shouldn't depend on your guess. The Poisson model avoids this entirely — it only needs the rate.

When n IS known and large, and p is small, binomial gives you nearly the same answer as Poisson (because Binomial(1000, 0.008) ≈ Poisson(8)). But if you genuinely know n, the binomial is more informative because it uses that information.

Your professor's answer isn't wrong, but it's incomplete. Let me unpack when the CLT actually applies and when the Normal distribution is appropriate.

**The Central Limit Theorem, concretely**

If you take n independent draws from ANY distribution with finite mean mu and finite variance sigma^2, the sample mean X-bar is approximately Normal(mu, sigma^2/n) when n is large enough.

"Large enough" depends on how non-Normal the original distribution is:
- Original is symmetric, light-tailed: n > 15 is usually fine
- Original is moderately skewed: n > 30 is the textbook rule
- Original is heavily skewed or has outliers: n > 100, maybe more
- Original has infinite variance (Cauchy, Pareto with alpha < 2): **CLT never applies.** No sample size helps.

**Three situations where you use Normal:**

1. **The data is genuinely Normal.** Height of adult humans, measurement error from a well-calibrated instrument, IQ scores. These arise when the variable is the sum of many small, independent effects. Height = sum of ~400 genetic contributions plus environmental noise. Each is small, they're roughly independent, and the CLT explains why the sum is approximately Normal.

2. **You're analyzing a sample mean or proportion.** Even if individual data points aren't Normal, the *average* of n points often is. You sampled 50 customer wait times (skewed, not Normal), but the *mean* wait time follows an approximately Normal distribution. This is the CLT at work on your estimator, not your data.

3. **You're doing a hypothesis test or building a confidence interval** that relies on Normality of the test statistic. The t-test, z-test, and most regression inference assumes Normal residuals or Normal sampling distributions.

**When Normal is wrong (common traps):**

- **Bounded data:** Percentages (0-100%), proportions (0-1). Normal assigns nonzero probability outside these bounds. Use Beta or logit-Normal instead.
- **Count data:** Number of accidents, defects, goals. Normal allows negative values and non-integers. Use Poisson or Negative Binomial.
- **Heavy-tailed data:** Financial returns, insurance claims, earthquake magnitudes. The tails of the Normal decay like e^(-x^2), which is much too fast for data where extreme events occur more often than the Normal predicts. Use t-distribution, log-Normal, or Pareto.
- **Skewed data:** Income, home prices, survival times. The Normal is symmetric; these are right-skewed. Often log-Normal works (take the log, get a Normal).

**The practical test:** Plot your data. If the histogram is roughly bell-shaped and symmetric, Normal is reasonable. If you see skew, heavy tails, or hard boundaries, it's not. A QQ-plot (plotting your data quantiles against Normal quantiles) makes this visual — if the points follow a straight line, Normal fits; deviations at the ends indicate heavy tails or skew.

The GIL is the wrong mental model here. Async code runs on a single thread, so the GIL isn't relevant — but `await` is a **cooperative yield point**, and that's a different kind of hazard.

I'd bet your handler looks roughly like this:

```python
async def handle_event(event: Event) -> None:
    current = counters.get(event.tenant_id, 0)
    enriched = await enrich(event)      # <-- yield point
    await save(enriched)                # <-- yield point
    counters[event.tenant_id] = current + 1
```

Two events for the same tenant, A and B, interleave:

```
A: reads counters["tenant42"] = 100
A: awaits enrich() -- yields
B: reads counters["tenant42"] = 100     <-- sees stale value
B: awaits enrich() -- yields
A: resumes, awaits save() -- yields
B: resumes, awaits save() -- yields
A: writes counters["tenant42"] = 101
B: writes counters["tenant42"] = 101     <-- should have been 102
```

One increment vanishes. At 5 events/sec with varied tenants, collisions are rare. At 50k events replayed fast, the same-tenant arrival rate on hot tenants climbs and you get ~0.3% loss. That number tracks.

## Minimal repro that reliably fails

```python
import asyncio

counter: dict[str, int] = {}

async def inc_unsafe(key: str) -> None:
    current = counter.get(key, 0)
    await asyncio.sleep(0)               # any await exposes the race
    counter[key] = current + 1

async def main() -> None:
    await asyncio.gather(*(inc_unsafe("k") for _ in range(10_000)))
    print(f"expected 10000, got {counter['k']}")

asyncio.run(main())
# prints: expected 10000, got 1
```

Yes, 1. Every coroutine reads 0, yields, writes 1.

## The GIL question

The GIL makes `dict[key] += 1` safe **between threads** because `INPLACE_ADD` isn't a yield point in bytecode. But in a single-threaded async loop, the hazard isn't mid-bytecode preemption — it's `await`. Any `await` between your read and your write is a window where another coroutine on the same thread can run and stomp on you. Rule of thumb:

> **If there is no `await` between the read and the write, the operation is safe.**

That's why `counter[k] += 1` by itself is fine in async — no yield point.

## Fixes, in order of preference

**1. Restructure so the increment has no intervening await.**

```python
async def handle_event(event: Event) -> None:
    enriched = await enrich(event)
    await save(enriched)
    counters[event.tenant_id] = counters.get(event.tenant_id, 0) + 1   # no await between
```

Often the cleanest fix. Do the side effect when you know the result, not speculatively.

**2. Per-tenant lock if you really need the counter available during the await.**

```python
from collections import defaultdict

locks: dict[str, asyncio.Lock] = defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)

async def handle_event(event: Event) -> None:
    async with locks[event.tenant_id]:
        current = counters.get(event.tenant_id, 0)
        enriched = await enrich(event)
        await save(enriched)
        counters[event.tenant_id] = current + 1
```

Note: `defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)` has its own race — two coroutines asking for a lock for a new tenant at the same time may each create one. For correctness, guard creation with a top-level lock or use `asyncio.Lock` lazily in a helper that checks-then-creates inside a global mutex. For most workloads the `defaultdict` version is fine because lock creation is fast and the window is tiny.

**3. Accumulate locally, flush atomically.**

```python
local_counts: Counter[str] = Counter()

async def handle_event(event: Event) -> None:
    enriched = await enrich(event)
    await save(enriched)
    local_counts[event.tenant_id] += 1    # safe: no await after the increment
```

Best when you don't need a live global view. Periodically merge `local_counts` into your metrics backend.

Pick option 1 when you can. It's the one that scales, needs no locks, and makes the hazard structurally impossible.

This pattern is almost always one of two things in a Rails + PgBouncer transaction-mode setup: a **prepared statement storm** or a **connection storm**. Given the stack, my strong prior is prepared statements. Here's why and how to confirm.

## Why prepared statements hurt you here

Rails 7.x defaults to `prepared_statements: true`. The ActiveRecord pattern is: send `PREPARE stmt_1 AS SELECT ...`, then on subsequent calls send `EXECUTE stmt_1(...)`. Prepared statements live on a specific Postgres **backend** (process) and are deallocated when that backend disconnects.

In **PgBouncer transaction mode**, your Rails connection does *not* own a Postgres backend. PgBouncer hands you whatever backend is free for the duration of one transaction, then releases it. The next transaction might land on a completely different backend — which has never seen your `PREPARE stmt_1`. So the `EXECUTE` errors out, Rails re-prepares, next transaction goes to yet another backend, re-prepares again.

Post-deploy, all your Rails connection pools are cold. Every unique query shape gets prepared on every PgBouncer backend as traffic fans out. That's a *lot* of parse + plan work concentrated into the first minutes after boot. Parsing and planning is CPU-heavy on PG — much more so than executing a cached plan.

Note: Rails + PgBouncer transaction mode has been a known footgun for years. Many shops run this way "fine" because Rails has defensive code to handle the `prepared statement "xxx" does not exist` error, but the cost of that recovery is exactly what you're seeing.

## Confirm it in 5 minutes

**1. During the next spike (or replay a restart in staging), run:**

```sql
-- How much of the load is actually PREPARE/DEALLOCATE?
SELECT query, calls, total_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE query ILIKE 'PREPARE%' OR query ILIKE 'DEALLOCATE%'
ORDER BY calls DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Compare against total
SELECT sum(calls) FROM pg_stat_statements;
```

If PREPARE/DEALLOCATE is >10% of calls during the spike (and <1% in steady state), that's your diagnosis, full stop.

**2. Check for the error in PG logs:**

```bash
grep 'prepared statement' /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-15-main.log | tail
```

You'll see lines like `ERROR: prepared statement "a1" does not exist`. If these cluster around deploys, confirmed.

**3. Check PgBouncer backend churn:**

```
pgbouncer=# SHOW POOLS;
-- look at sv_active, sv_idle, sv_used during the spike
pgbouncer=# SHOW STATS;
-- total_xact_count vs total_query_count — a ratio <<1 means many queries per transaction, which is fine; a ratio ~1 means every query is its own transaction (worse for prep-statement reuse)
```

## Fixes, lowest-risk first

**Fix 1: Disable prepared statements in Rails (recommended for PgBouncer transaction mode).**

In `config/database.yml`:

```yaml
production:
  adapter: postgresql
  prepared_statements: false
  advisory_locks: false  # also misbehaves with transaction pooling
  # ...
```

You lose roughly 5-15% per-query overhead vs a cached plan. In exchange you eliminate the post-deploy spike and a class of sporadic production errors. Almost every team I know on Rails + PgBouncer transaction mode runs this way. It's the right trade.

**Fix 2: Upgrade PgBouncer to 1.21+ and turn on protocol-level prepared statement tracking.**

PgBouncer 1.21 (2023) added real support for prepared statements in transaction mode via the extended query protocol. Set:

```ini
[pgbouncer]
max_prepared_statements = 100
```

This makes PgBouncer itself track prepared statements across backends and re-prepare lazily. If you can upgrade, this is the nicest fix — you keep the performance benefit of prepared statements. Verify your driver uses the extended protocol (pg gem and the `pg` driver do by default in recent versions).

**Fix 3: Switch PgBouncer to session mode.**

Prepared statements work fine in session mode because each client holds a backend for its whole session. The downside is you lose most of PgBouncer's pooling benefit — you need `pool_size` ≈ your app's total connection count. Only do this if you have low connection fan-out.

## Also: check for a connection storm

Even with prepared statements fixed, a burst of new connections at deploy time adds CPU. If you roll all app pods at once, PgBouncer may need to open many new server connections simultaneously. Two mitigations:

```yaml
# database.yml — keep pool small per instance
pool: 5   # not 25. With transaction mode, 5 is plenty per process.
```

```yaml
# k8s deployment
spec:
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 10%        # not 25% or 100%
      maxUnavailable: 0
  minReadySeconds: 15      # give each wave time to warm
```

Staggered rollout flattens the spike from a 60-second peak into a smooth ramp.

## The order I'd do this

1. Flip `prepared_statements: false` in a staging deploy. Measure the spike — it should disappear or shrink dramatically.
2. If it does, ship it to prod during a calm window. You're done for now.
3. Independently, reduce `maxSurge` on your deployment to stagger the connection ramp.
4. Schedule a PgBouncer 1.21 upgrade for next quarter if you care about the prepared-statement performance.

**Layer 1: phase-aware limit bumps.**

Have the job signal its runtime before entering the reduce phase. The runtime bumps `memory.max` for the duration and reverts after. On cgroup v2 you can raise it freely; lowering requires the current usage to already be below the new target (or the kernel will try to reclaim and potentially OOM).

A simple controller:

```rust
// Job emits: "entering_final_reduce", expected_peak=40G, max_duration=60s
use std::fs;
use std::time::Duration;

fn bump_cgroup(path: &str, target: &str, window: Duration) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let max_path = format!("{}/memory.max", path);
    let prev = fs::read_to_string(&max_path)?.trim().to_string();
    fs::write(&max_path, target)?;
    // spawn a watchdog that reverts if the job doesn't signal completion
    let max_path = max_path.clone();
    let prev = prev.clone();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        std::thread::sleep(window);
        // Only safe to lower once current < prev. Check memory.current first.
        let cur: u64 = fs::read_to_string(max_path.replace("memory.max", "memory.current"))
            .ok().and_then(|s| s.trim().parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0);
        let prev_val: u64 = prev.parse().unwrap_or(u64::MAX);
        if cur < prev_val {
            let _ = fs::write(&max_path, prev);
        } // else: job is still using bump — let it ride or oom-group-kill
    });
    Ok(())
}
```

Key constraints:
- **Bounded window.** The bump auto-reverts after N seconds. A misbehaving job can't lie about entering reduce and hold the bump forever.
- **Bounded concurrency.** The runtime tracks total bumped capacity across jobs and refuses bumps that would overcommit the host. Backpressure → the job waits.
- **oom.group=1 is critical.** If a job claims it needs 40GB, gets the bump, and then keeps climbing past 40G, the bumped memory.max still OOM-kills the whole cgroup. The bump is generous, not infinite.
- **Lowering the limit.** Attempting to lower memory.max below memory.current does synchronous reclaim in the writer's context and can return ENOMEM without OOMing the target. Check memory.current first, as shown.

**Layer 2: swap as the escape valve for unexpected spikes.**

Even with bumps, set `memory.swap.max` generously (e.g., 16G per job). With zswap enabled, a job that briefly overshoots lands in compressed RAM — milliseconds of slowdown, not OOM. For your 30-second reduce, if it peaks 5% above the bumped max, swap absorbs it invisibly.

```ini
MemoryHigh=16G
MemoryMax=24G      # normal cap
MemorySwapMax=16G  # escape valve
# During reduce: controller writes 40G to memory.max
```

**Layer 3: proactive reclaim on neighbors (6.1+).**

Before granting a 40G bump, tell colocated jobs to shed cold pages:

```
$ echo 2G > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/batch@other.service/memory.reclaim
```

This triggers background reclaim of up to 2GB from that cgroup — evicts clean page cache, pushes cold anonymous pages to zswap. The neighbor doesn't die; it just loses some cached state. Combined with the bump, you move headroom to where it's needed without per-job overcommit.

**What not to do:**

- Don't set `memory.max` at the peak globally — you've already identified why.
- Don't rely on `memory.high` alone. High throttles but doesn't kill, so a true leak sits there consuming all the host RAM via swap forever.
- Don't try to coordinate via oom_score_adj — v2 doesn't really care, and cgroup-scoped OOM is the right boundary anyway.

**Test it:**

```
# Simulate a job that legitimately spikes
stress-ng --vm 1 --vm-bytes 35G --vm-keep --timeout 30 &
# Verify memory.max got bumped, check memory.events during and after
watch -n0.5 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.{current,max,events}'
```

You should see `memory.max` change from 24G to 40G during the window, `memory.current` climb to ~35G, then both return. `high` counter may tick a bit around the transition — that's fine, it means the throttle worked before the bump took effect.

The net effect: well-behaved jobs get their legitimate peaks, misbehaving jobs are bounded to their normal cap + swap, and the host is never at risk.

Context managers (the `with` statement) ensure setup and cleanup code runs even if exceptions occur. They're Python's answer to resource management.

**The problem they solve:**
```python
# Without context manager — easy to forget cleanup
f = open('file.txt')
try:
    data = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()  # Must remember this

# With context manager — cleanup is automatic
with open('file.txt') as f:
    data = f.read()
# f.close() called automatically, even on exception
```

**Writing custom context managers (two approaches):**

**Approach 1: Class with __enter__ and __exit__:**
```python
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self  # This is what 'as' binds to

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"Elapsed: {self.elapsed:.3f}s")
        return False  # Don't suppress exceptions

with Timer() as t:
    slow_function()
print(f"Took {t.elapsed:.3f}s")
```

**Approach 2: Generator with @contextmanager (simpler):**
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def temp_directory():
    dirpath = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    try:
        yield dirpath  # Everything before yield is __enter__
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(dirpath)  # Everything after yield is __exit__

with temp_directory() as tmpdir:
    # tmpdir exists and is usable
    create_files_in(tmpdir)
# tmpdir is automatically deleted
```

**Async context managers:**
```python
@asynccontextmanager
async def db_transaction(session):
    try:
        yield session
        await session.commit()
    except Exception:
        await session.rollback()
        raise

async with db_transaction(session) as s:
    await s.execute(insert_stmt)
    # Commits on success, rolls back on exception
```

**Common use cases:**
- File handling (open/close)
- Database transactions (begin/commit/rollback)
- Locks (acquire/release)
- Temporary state changes (modify/restore)
- Network connections (connect/disconnect)
- Timing and profiling
- Redirecting stdout/stderr

A bare syscall on Skylake+ with KPTI + IBRS + retpolines runs roughly:
- KPTI page table swap on entry/exit: ~100-150ns (TLB cost)
- IBRS write on entry: ~80-150ns
- Retpoline indirect calls: ~30-60ns

```c
#include <liburing.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#define N 1000
#define BUFSZ 4096

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    int fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
    struct io_uring ring;
    if (io_uring_queue_init(N, &ring, 0) < 0) return 1;

    char *bufs[N];
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) bufs[i] = aligned_alloc(4096, BUFSZ);

    // Submit N reads -- zero syscalls so far, just SQE writes
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
        io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, bufs[i], BUFSZ, i * BUFSZ);
        io_uring_sqe_set_data(sqe, bufs[i]);
    }

    // ONE syscall to kick the kernel
    io_uring_submit(&ring);

    // Reap completions (no syscall if CQE already there, otherwise one io_uring_enter)
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        struct io_uring_cqe *cqe;
        io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
        if (cqe->res < 0) fprintf(stderr, "read failed: %d\n", cqe->res);
        io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);
    }

    io_uring_queue_exit(&ring);
    return 0;
}
```

For cold disk I/O, the syscall overhead is rounding error against millisecond-scale I/O wait, and io_uring's advantage shifts to *concurrency* (issuing 1000 reads to NVMe in parallel without 1000 threads).

```c
struct io_uring_params p = {0};
p.flags = IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL;
p.sq_thread_idle = 2000;  // ms before kernel thread sleeps
```

```typescript
    console.log(r.data.name);  // no ?, no !, no narrowing dance
  } else {

    console.error(r.error);
  }

```

```typescript
  | { status: 'loading' }

  | { status: 'error'; error: string; retryable: boolean };
```

With Zod (recommended for non-trivial APIs):

```typescript
import { z } from 'zod';

const WireResponse = z.object({
  status: z.enum(['success', 'error']),
  data: z.object({ id: z.string(), name: z.string() }).optional(),
  error: z.string().optional(),
});

type Response =
  | { status: 'success'; data: User }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string };

function parseResponse(raw: unknown): Response {
  const wire = WireResponse.parse(raw);  // throws on schema mismatch
  if (wire.status === 'success') {
    if (!wire.data) throw new Error('success response missing data');
    return { status: 'success', data: wire.data };
  }
  if (!wire.error) throw new Error('error response missing error');
  return { status: 'error', error: wire.error };
}

async function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<Response> {
  const raw = await fetch(`/users/${id}`).then(r => r.json());
  return parseResponse(raw);
}
```

No dependency? Hand-roll the same idea — it's tiny:

```typescript
function parseResponse(raw: unknown): Response {
  if (typeof raw !== 'object' || raw === null) {
    throw new Error('response is not an object');
  }
  const r = raw as Record<string, unknown>;
  if (r.status === 'success' && r.data) {
    return { status: 'success', data: r.data as User };
  }
  if (r.status === 'error' && typeof r.error === 'string') {
    return { status: 'error', error: r.error };
  }
  throw new Error('malformed response');
}
```

Three levels of enforcement, pick what fits:

**Level 1 (easiest): gitignore go.work entirely.** This is the Go team's default recommendation. go.work is meant to be a developer-local convenience for working on multiple modules at once. If you commit it, you're saying "every developer must use this exact workspace setup," which is rarely true.

```
# .gitignore

go.work.sum
```

If someone needs a workspace, they create one locally; it never affects CI or other developers.

**Level 2: build with `GOWORK=off` in CI.** Belt and suspenders — even if go.work sneaks in, CI ignores it:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
env:
  GOWORK: off
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
    with: { go-version: '1.24' }
  - run: go build ./...
  - run: go test ./...
```

This guarantees CI uses go.mod as the single source of truth. A developer's local go.work can never affect CI results. I'd recommend this regardless of whether you also do level 1.

**Level 3 (if you must commit go.work): lint it.** Sometimes monorepos legitimately commit go.work because the workspace structure is part of the project. In that case, you want to forbid local-path replaces:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lint-goworkspace.sh
set -euo pipefail

if [ ! -f go.work ]; then
  exit 0
fi

# Use go work edit -json for structured parsing instead of regex on the file
bad=$(go work edit -json | jq -r '
  .Replace // [] | .[] |
  select(
    .New.Path | test("^(\\.|/|[A-Z]:\\\\)")
  ) |
  "\(.Old.Path) => \(.New.Path)"
')

if [ -n "$bad" ]; then
  echo "go.work contains local-path replaces, which cannot be committed:"
  echo "$bad"
  echo ""
  echo "Use a module-path replace, or move this to a developer-local go.work"
  echo "that is not committed to the repo."
  exit 1
fi

# Also forbid use directives that point outside the repo
bad_use=$(go work edit -json | jq -r '
  .Use // [] | .[] |
  select(.DiskPath | test("^(/|\\.\\./|[A-Z]:\\\\)")) |
  .DiskPath
')

if [ -n "$bad_use" ]; then
  echo "go.work has 'use' directives outside repo:"
  echo "$bad_use"
  exit 1
fi
```

I should also mention that Django's QuerySet is lazy, so the `filter` in the loop is creating new queries each time rather than filtering in memory.

You have a 1 + 3N query problem. With 30 projects, that is 91 separate database round trips. Here is what is happening on each loop iteration:

1. `Task.objects.filter(project=project)` -- creates a queryset (lazy, not a hit yet)
2. `.count()` -- hits the database (query 1)
3. `.filter(status='open').count()` -- hits the database again (query 2)
4. `project.members.all()` -- hits the database for the M2M join (query 3)

**Refactored: 2 queries total**

```python
from django.db.models import Count, Q
from django.http import JsonResponse


def dashboard(request):
    projects = (
        Project.objects.filter(owner=request.user)
        .annotate(
            task_count=Count("task"),
            open_task_count=Count("task", filter=Q(task__status="open")),
        )
        .prefetch_related("members")
    )

    result = [
        {
            "project": project.name,
            "task_count": project.task_count,
            "open_tasks": project.open_task_count,
            "members": [m.username for m in project.members.all()],
        }
        for project in projects
    ]
    return JsonResponse({"projects": result})
```

**What changed:**

- `annotate` with `Count` pushes both counts into a single SQL query with conditional aggregation. The database computes `task_count` and `open_task_count` as part of the project fetch -- no per-project round trips.
- `prefetch_related("members")` fetches all member relationships in a second query and caches them in memory. The `.all()` call inside the list comprehension hits the prefetch cache, not the database.

This should drop from 91 queries to 2, and your 4-second response should drop to under 100ms.

The query "wireless noise cancelling headphones under $200 with good bass" needs to be parsed into:

- Category: headphones
- Attributes: wireless=true, noise_cancelling=true

- Soft preferences: bass_quality=high

2. **Entity extraction** — recognize category ("headphones"), brand, model, attribute values ("wireless", "noise cancelling").
3. **Numeric/range extraction** — "under $200" → price < 200; "size 10" → size = 10.

```python
        for attr_name, attr_values in info.get("attributes", {}).items():
```

**The decision rule for index vs. query time**

- The transformation is expensive and would slow every query (e.g., generating n-grams for prefix matching).
- The transformation is universal — it should apply identically to every document and every query (lowercasing, ASCII folding).
- The transformation produces tokens you genuinely want in the index.

Do it at query time when:

- You want to change it without reindexing (synonym lists, weights).
- It depends on context the index doesn't have (user locale, A/B test variant).

```json
          "tokenizer": "standard",

      },
      "filter": {

```

- Bake in the things you're confident about: lowercasing, ASCII folding, basic stemming. These rarely change.

They're orthogonal layers, not alternatives. They solve different problems.

**Definitions, sharpened**

- **Query understanding** = parsing a natural-language query into a structured representation. Intent, entities, attributes, ranges. Pre-processing.
- **Semantic search** = retrieval based on learned meaning rather than lexical token match. Dense vector retrieval over neural embeddings. Retrieval method.

Query understanding is at the front of the pipeline; retrieval methods sit further down. You can combine query understanding with any retrieval — lexical, semantic, or both.

**Concrete examples to make this concrete**

Query: `wireless noise cancelling headphones under $200 with good bass`

- Query understanding alone (no semantic): produces `{filters: {wireless: true, noise_cancelling: true}, constraint: price<200, free_text: "good bass"}` and issues this to BM25. "Good bass" matches docs that contain those tokens. Misses docs that say "deep low-end response" instead.
- Semantic search alone (no QU): embeds the entire query as one vector, searches dense vectors. Finds conceptually similar products including ones with "deep low-end response" — but doesn't enforce the price filter, so $400 headphones might rank in your top-10. Brittle.
- Both: QU peels off the filters and constraint. The remaining `"good bass"` is embedded and searches the dense index. BM25 also runs on it. Hybrid fusion combines. Filters are enforced as hard constraints in both retrievers.

The "both" version handles vocabulary mismatch (semantic) AND respects structured constraints (QU) AND has lexical backstops for exact-match queries (BM25).

**Where query understanding alone is sufficient**

- Strict product search with well-curated taxonomy.
- Most queries are short and category/brand/attribute-based.
- Users don't paraphrase much (e.g., they search "nike air max 90 size 10" not "those white nike sneakers I saw").
- Catalog vocabulary matches user vocabulary closely.

**Where you need semantic on top**

- Vocabulary mismatch — user says "cancel subscription," doc says "unsubscribe." Synonym dictionaries patch known cases; semantic handles the novel ones.
- Conceptual queries — "books like Project Hail Mary," "songs that sound like Radiohead." No entity to extract; only meaning matters.
- FAQ and support search — natural-language questions where no taxonomy can enumerate all phrasings.
- Long content discovery — finding articles, videos, podcasts where titles/descriptions don't always match user intent literally.

**Where you need lexical on top of semantic**

This often gets missed. Pure semantic search has its own failures:

- Exact-match queries — `iPhone 15 Pro Max 256GB` should return that exact product, not semantically similar phones. Dense retrieval can be off by one digit in a model number.
- Brand/SKU queries where lexical exactness matters.
- Very short queries (1-2 tokens) where embedding quality is poor due to lack of context.

This is why hybrid (BM25 + dense + RRF) is the modern default — neither retriever alone covers all cases. Query understanding helps both.

**Practical layering**

```
User query
    ↓
Query understanding
    ├─ extract filters → applied to both retrievers as hard constraints
    └─ free-text remainder
         ↓
         ├─→ BM25 retrieval (top-100)
         └─→ Dense retrieval (top-100)
              ↓
              RRF fusion → top-50
              ↓
              Cross-encoder rerank → top-20
              ↓
              Apply business rules (boost/diversify)
              ↓
              Return
```

Query understanding sits at the front and feeds structured filters to all retrievers. The retrieval mix is chosen by failure-mode coverage: lexical handles exact match, semantic handles vocabulary mismatch, fusion handles the long tail of cases where one is right and the other isn't.

**The practical answer to your question**

If you only ship one thing on top of BM25, ship query understanding (filter/range/entity extraction) — the relevance lift on long natural-language queries is dramatic and immediate. If you only ship a second thing, ship hybrid retrieval (add a dense retriever, fuse with RRF). The rerank layer comes third. They compound; each one targets failures the others can't fix.

Raft breaks consensus into three problems. Here is each one with the invariant that makes it correct.

**1. Leader election**

Every node is in one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader. Time is divided into terms (monotonically increasing integers).

- Followers listen for heartbeats from the leader. If no heartbeat arrives within a randomized timeout (150-300ms typically), the follower becomes a candidate.
- A candidate increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from all other nodes.
- A node grants its vote if: (a) it has not already voted in this term, and (b) the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own.
- A candidate that receives votes from a majority becomes leader. It immediately sends heartbeats to establish authority.

**Critical invariant:** Condition (b) guarantees that any elected leader contains all committed entries. A committed entry exists on a majority. A candidate needs a majority to win. Those two majorities must overlap, so at least one voter has the committed entry and will reject a candidate without it.

**2. Log replication**

The leader receives client requests, appends them to its log, and replicates to followers via `AppendEntries` RPCs.

```
Leader log:     [1:set x=1] [1:set y=2] [2:set x=3]
                 term 1       term 1       term 2

AppendEntries to Follower B:
  prevLogIndex=2, prevLogTerm=1, entries=[{term:2, cmd:set x=3}]

Follower B checks: does my log[2] have term 1? 
  Yes → append entry, reply success
  No  → reply failure, leader decrements prevLogIndex and retries
```

An entry is **committed** once the leader has replicated it to a majority. The leader then applies it to its state machine and responds to the client.

**Critical invariant:** The log matching property. If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, all preceding entries are identical. This is enforced by the consistency check in `AppendEntries`.

**3. Safety**

Two rules prevent the system from reaching an inconsistent state:

- **Election restriction:** A candidate's log must be at least as up-to-date as the voter's (compared by last entry's term, then length). This prevents stale nodes from becoming leader.
- **Commit rule:** A leader only commits entries from its own term by counting replicas. Entries from previous terms are committed indirectly when a current-term entry after them is committed. This prevents a subtle bug where an entry replicated to a majority could still be overwritten.

**In practice (3-node cluster):**
- Majority = 2. One node can fail and the cluster continues.
- Write latency = 1 round trip (leader to one follower).
- If the leader dies, election takes ~300-500ms (timeout + vote round).
- 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures but has higher write latency (needs 2 follower ACKs).

That is the entire core algorithm. The paper's remaining 30 pages cover log compaction (snapshotting to bound log growth), cluster membership changes (adding/removing nodes safely), and correctness proofs.

### Week 1: Stop the bleed

```bash

```

**1b. Rotate every one of those secrets.** DB password, any API keys (Stripe, AWS, SendGrid, whatever), signing keys, everything. If you rotated some of them already, great — rotate the rest.

**1c. Purge headers from logs immediately.** Pick your framework's middleware and redact Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key, Proxy-Authorization at source *before* the log line is constructed. Don't rely on Datadog-side scrubbing alone — defense in depth.

```python
# FastAPI / Starlette example
REDACT_HEADERS = {"authorization", "cookie", "x-api-key", "proxy-authorization", "x-csrf-token"}

def safe_headers(h):
    return {k: ("[REDACTED]" if k.lower() in REDACT_HEADERS else v) for k, v in h.items()}

# Use safe_headers(request.headers) anywhere you log.
```

**1d. Add a Datadog log processing rule as a second layer:**

```yaml
logs:

    - type: mask_sequences
      name: redact_bearer_tokens
      pattern: 'Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-]+'
      replace_placeholder: 'Bearer [REDACTED]'
```

### Week 2-3: Install a real secrets manager

Pick one: AWS Secrets Manager (if you're on AWS), GCP Secret Manager, or HashiCorp Vault. Skip HashiCorp Vault if your team is small — operational overhead isn't worth it for <20 engineers.

Pattern: services fetch secrets at startup AND on a background refresh interval, cache in memory only, never write to disk or log.

```python
import time, threading, boto3, json
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class SecretCache:
    value: str
    fetched_at: float

class Secrets:
    def __init__(self, region: str, ttl: int = 300):
        self._client = boto3.client("secretsmanager", region_name=region)
        self._ttl = ttl
        self._cache: dict[str, SecretCache] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def get(self, name: str) -> str:
        now = time.time()
        with self._lock:
            entry = self._cache.get(name)
            if entry and now - entry.fetched_at < self._ttl:
                return entry.value
        resp = self._client.get_secret_value(SecretId=name)
        value = json.loads(resp["SecretString"])["value"]
        with self._lock:
            self._cache[name] = SecretCache(value, now)
        return value

secrets = Secrets(region="us-east-1")

# Usage - no more import-time env var:
def charge_card(token: str, amount: int):
    stripe.api_key = secrets.get("prod/stripe/api_key")
    return stripe.Charge.create(...)
```

The 300s TTL means a rotation propagates within 5 minutes with no restart.

### Week 3-4: Automated rotation

- RDS: enable Secrets Manager automatic rotation, 30-day cadence.
- Stripe: quarterly manual rotation, calendar entry, documented runbook.
- Internal service-to-service: short-lived tokens issued per request (mTLS or JWT with 5-min expiry), no long-lived shared secrets at all.

### Week 4: GitHub Actions hardening

- Replace static AWS/GCP keys with OIDC federation. `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4` supports this natively.
- Add environment protection rules on any workflow that touches production: required reviewers, branch restrictions.
- Audit every `pull_request` triggered workflow — none should have access to production secrets. Use `pull_request_target` with extreme care (there's a whole class of exploits here — see GitHub's own guidance on script injection via PR title/body).

### Ongoing

- Pre-commit hook: `gitleaks protect --staged` or `ggshield pre-commit` to catch secret commits before they land.
- Quarterly access review: who has secrets-manager IAM permissions, who has Datadog read access, who has PaaS dashboard access.
- Incident runbook for "suspected key exposure" — rotation steps per secret type, who's notified, what gets logged.

The SOC 2 auditor will specifically ask about: rotation cadence (document it), access logs (Secrets Manager has them, PaaS dashboards often don't), and your process for handling exposed credentials. The git history exposure is the thing they'll dock you for if you haven't addressed it with rotation + documented timeline.

A memory leak occurs when a program retains references to objects it no longer needs, preventing the garbage collector from reclaiming them. In GC'd languages, it's not that memory isn't freed — it's that the program unintentionally keeps it reachable.

**Common causes in Python/JavaScript:**

1. **Global collections that grow without bounds:**
```python
cache = {}  # Global dict that never gets entries removed
def process(key, data):
    cache[key] = expensive_transform(data)  # Cache grows forever
```
Fix: Use `functools.lru_cache` with a maxsize, or a WeakValueDictionary, or explicit eviction.

2. **Closures capturing large objects:**
```javascript
function createHandler(largeData) {
    return function() {
        console.log(largeData.length); // closure keeps largeData alive
    };
}
```
The handler function keeps `largeData` in memory as long as the handler exists.

3. **Event listeners not cleaned up:**
```javascript
element.addEventListener('click', handler);
// If element is removed from DOM but handler references it, neither is GC'd
```
Fix: `removeEventListener` when done, or use `{ once: true }`.

4. **Circular references with weak areas of the GC:** Less common in modern GCs, but C extensions in Python or native modules in Node can create reference cycles the GC can't detect.

**How to find leaks:**

**Python:**
```python
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()

# ... run your code ...

snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snapshot.statistics('lineno')[:10]:
    print(stat)  # Shows which lines allocated the most memory

# Or use objgraph
import objgraph
objgraph.show_growth()  # Shows which object types are increasing
```

**JavaScript/Node:**
```bash
node --inspect app.js  # Then use Chrome DevTools → Memory tab
# Take heap snapshots at different times, compare to find growing object counts
```

**The process:**
1. Monitor memory over time (RSS or heap size). If it grows without bound under steady load, you have a leak.
2. Take heap snapshots at two points and compare: which object types increased?
3. Trace the retaining references back to the root: what's keeping these objects alive?
4. Fix the retention path (remove from collection, remove listener, break reference).

ACID guarantees reliable transaction processing:

**Atomicity:** A transaction is all-or-nothing. If any part fails, everything is rolled back.
```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;  -- Both succeed or both fail
```

**Consistency:** A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints (foreign keys, unique, check) are always enforced.

**Isolation:** Concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. Isolation levels control the trade-off:
- **Read Uncommitted:** Can see uncommitted changes (dirty reads)
- **Read Committed:** Only see committed data (default in PostgreSQL)
- **Repeatable Read:** Same query returns same results within a transaction
- **Serializable:** Transactions behave as if executed one at a time (slowest, safest)

**Durability:** Once committed, data survives crashes. Achieved via write-ahead logging (WAL) — changes are written to a log before the actual data files.

NoSQL databases often relax ACID for performance and scalability (BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency).

Here's the operational definition that does most of the work in physics:

> **A quantity is *topological* if it is invariant under continuous deformations of the underlying objects — fields, Hamiltonians, parameters — within a fixed class.**

The class matters: "gapped Hamiltonians," "nowhere-vanishing vector fields," "loops avoiding a singularity." Within that class, smooth tweaks don't change the invariant. That's why topological quantities are robust to disorder, perturbations, and details — they're the part of the physics that can't be smoothed away.

The invariants are integers (or elements of finite groups), because counting equivalence classes of continuous maps gives discrete answers.

## The atom of the subject: winding number

Consider a complex order parameter $\psi: S^1 \to \mathbb{C}^*$ that doesn't vanish, parametrized as $\psi(\theta) = |\psi(\theta)| e^{i\phi(\theta)}$. The phase $\phi$ is multivalued, but $\phi(2\pi) - \phi(0) = 2\pi n$ for some integer $n$ — the **winding number**:
$$n = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint \frac{d\psi}{\psi} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \oint d\phi.$$

Why is $n$ an integer? Because $\psi$ is single-valued at $\theta = 0 = 2\pi$. Why is $n$ a deformation invariant? If you continuously deform $\psi$ without it crossing zero, $n$ changes continuously — but it's an integer, so it can't change at all. The class is "non-vanishing $\psi$" and crossing zero is leaving the class.

This is $\pi_1(\mathbb{C}^*) = \pi_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ in physicist language. Vortices in superfluids, defects in nematic liquid crystals, kinks in 1D field theories — all live here.

## Where the integers come from in your examples

**Aharonov-Bohm:** the configuration space of an electron avoiding a flux tube in 2D is $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\} \simeq S^1$, with $\pi_1 = \mathbb{Z}$. Different paths around the tube fall into integer-labeled homotopy classes. The phase $\exp(i e \Phi / \hbar)$ picked up around the tube depends only on the winding, not on the specific path. The flux $\Phi$ doesn't have to be a topological quantity — it's continuous — but the *path's* homotopy class is, and that's why interference patterns shift in quantized ways.

**Berry phase:** vary parameters $\mathbf{R}(t)$ along a loop in parameter space. The state picks up a geometric phase
$$\gamma = \oint_C \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{R}) \cdot d\mathbf{R}, \quad \mathbf{A} = i \langle n(\mathbf{R}) | \nabla_{\mathbf{R}} | n(\mathbf{R}) \rangle.$$
The connection $\mathbf{A}$ depends on a gauge choice for $|n(\mathbf{R})\rangle$. The line integral around a closed loop is gauge-invariant *modulo $2\pi$*. If you integrate the curvature (Berry curvature) over a closed surface, you get $2\pi \times \mathbb{Z}$ — the **Chern number** — which is genuinely a topological invariant of the bundle of states. Around a level-crossing degeneracy, the surrounding $S^2$ in parameter space carries Chern number $\pm 1$ — that's the magnetic monopole in parameter space.

**Topological insulators:** the Bloch Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{k})$ is a map from the Brillouin zone $T^d$ to the space of gapped Hermitian matrices. Two such maps are physically equivalent if they can be deformed into each other without closing the gap. The set of equivalence classes is labeled by topological invariants: Chern number for 2D Class A insulators, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariants for time-reversal-invariant insulators (the Kane-Mele invariant), and so on (the periodic table of topological insulators is the Bott periodicity of K-theory). Boundary modes are forced to exist because at a boundary, the bulk invariant has to change — and changing requires closing the gap, i.e., a metallic surface state.

## Concrete: the 2D Chern insulator

Take the simplest nontrivial example. A two-band Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{k}) = \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k}) \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}$, where $\mathbf{d}: T^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \{0\}$. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{d}} = \mathbf{d}/|\mathbf{d}|$ is a map $T^2 \to S^2$. The Chern number is
$$C = \frac{1}{4\pi} \int_{T^2} \hat{\mathbf{d}} \cdot (\partial_{k_x} \hat{\mathbf{d}} \times \partial_{k_y} \hat{\mathbf{d}}) \, d^2k,$$
which counts how many times $\hat{\mathbf{d}}$ wraps the sphere as $\mathbf{k}$ ranges over the BZ. Integer-valued, gauge-invariant, robust under any deformation that keeps $\mathbf{d} \ne 0$ (gap open). For the half-filled Haldane model, $C = \pm 1$ in the topological phase, and the Hall conductance is $C \cdot e^2/h$ — quantized exactly because $C$ is an integer that can't budge under perturbations.

## The slogan

*"Topological" in physics means: the answer is an integer (or discrete invariant) that doesn't change under any deformation that doesn't violate the rules.* The rules are usually "gap stays open" or "field stays nonzero" or "path avoids the singularity." Whenever you see a quantized response that's robust to disorder, look for a homotopy class hiding underneath.

1. Kubo formula gives Hall conductance as a sum over occupied bands of an integral of Berry curvature.
2. The integral over the BZ is the Chern number times $e^2/h$.

## The Kubo formula route (TKNN, 1982)

Linear response gives
$$\sigma_{xy} = \frac{e^2}{\hbar} \sum_{n \text{ filled}} \int_{\text{BZ}} \frac{d^2k}{(2\pi)^2} \, \Omega_n(\mathbf{k}),$$
where $\Omega_n = i (\partial_{k_x} \langle u_n | \partial_{k_y} u_n\rangle - (x \leftrightarrow y))$ is the Berry curvature of band $n$. The integral $\int \Omega_n / (2\pi) = C_n \in \mathbb{Z}$. So
$$\sigma_{xy} = \frac{e^2}{h} \sum_{n \text{ filled}} C_n.$$
The quantization isn't a derived fact — it's already there at the level of the Kubo formula, *provided* the Fermi level sits in a gap so the sum runs over a fixed set of bands.

## What does the work physically: Laughlin's flux-threading argument

This is the version that survives disorder. Roll the 2D sample into a cylinder, and adiabatically thread one flux quantum $\Phi_0 = h/e$ through the hole. The Hamiltonian at the start and end is gauge-equivalent — the spectrum is identical. But during the threading, charge is pumped from one edge to the other.

*How much charge?* If $C$ states cross the Fermi level per flux quantum (the spectral flow), then $C$ electrons are transferred. The voltage across the sample (from the EMF $-d\Phi/dt$) and the transferred current give
$$\sigma_{xy} = \frac{Q_{\text{transferred}}}{\Phi_0} = \frac{C e}{h/e} = C \frac{e^2}{h}.$$

The integer $C$ is the **Chern number**, recast as the number of states pumped across per flux quantum. The argument uses only:

1. Adiabaticity (gap stays open during threading).
2. Gauge invariance (final Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent to initial).
3. Charge conservation.

No translation invariance, no clean band structure. Disorder is fine as long as the bulk gap survives, which is why the IQHE plateaus are flat to one part in $10^9$ even in messy samples. The argument doesn't care about microscopic details — it's a topological accounting identity.

## What's *actually* doing the work

The spectral flow under flux threading is geometrically encoded by the curvature of the Bloch bundle over the BZ. "Curvature integrated over a closed surface = integer" is the Gauss-Bonnet/Chern-Weil theorem. Physics gives that closed surface (BZ torus + the closing-up under flux threading) automatically.

So the chain is: **bulk gap $\Rightarrow$ adiabatic theorem applies $\Rightarrow$ flux threading pumps an integer charge $\Rightarrow$ Hall conductance is $Ce^2/h$.** Each link is robust to perturbations that don't close the gap. That's why the plateau is exactly quantized: not because nature loves integers, but because charge conservation + gap + adiabaticity force the response to count an integer-valued geometric quantity.

The cleanest one-line physical picture: **the Chern number is the number of electrons pumped per flux quantum in a Thouless pump.** Everything else is bookkeeping.

- Treating clicks as ground truth without bias correction
- Optimizing offline metrics without validating online correlation
- No slice-based monitoring (head dominates aggregate, tail regressions invisible)
- Refreshing judgments too rarely (catalog drift makes labels wrong)

**Online component 1: A/B testing**

- **Search abandonment rate** (left without clicking) — direction is reversed (lower is better)

```python
def tdi_interleave(list_a: list, list_b: list, k: int = 10) -> tuple[list, list]:
    """Returns (interleaved_list, source_attributions)."""
    result, attribution = [], []
    iter_a, iter_b = iter(list_a), iter(list_b)
    seen = set()
    flip = random.random() < 0.5
    while len(result) < k:
        for source, it in (("A", iter_a), ("B", iter_b)) if flip else (("B", iter_b), ("A", iter_a)):
            doc = next((d for d in it if d not in seen), None)
            if doc:
                result.append(doc)
                attribution.append(source)
                seen.add(doc)
            if len(result) >= k:
                break
        flip = not flip
    return result, attribution
```

Log clicks with attribution. Aggregate over many users: if A's docs got more clicks than B's, A wins. Use a sign test for significance. This works for ranking but **not** for retrieval changes (different result sets) — for those, you need A/B.

**The correlation step (most teams skip this)**

At least once a quarter, run a known online win and verify it moved your offline metric in the same direction. If you had a 2% conversion rate lift online but offline NDCG@10 was flat, your offline eval doesn't reflect what users care about. Common causes: judgment set is stale, query set is unrepresentative, metric is wrong (using NDCG when MRR would catch the change).

**Build order recommendation**

1. Week 1-2: Pick a frozen query set (stratified, ~500 queries).
2. Week 2-4: Get baseline judgments — start click-derived with bias correction so you can move quickly. Plan human rating budget for the head.
3. Week 4: Wire offline metrics into CI. Every ranker change runs the eval; results posted to PR.
4. Week 6: Set up A/B framework with primary metrics.
5. Week 10+: Add interleaving for fast ranking iteration.
6. Ongoing: refresh judgments on a quarterly cadence, run online↔offline correlation checks.

The single most valuable habit: treat your eval system as a first-class product. It is the lens through which every future search improvement will be judged.

IPW (Inverse Propensity Weighting) for click data: the idea is that a click at rank 1 is much more likely than a click at rank 10 even for equally-relevant docs, because users see rank 1 more (examination probability is higher at top positions). To recover an unbiased estimate of relevance, weight each click by 1/P(examined | rank).

The steps:

1. **Estimate the propensity / examination probability per rank**. This is the probability that a user examined the doc at that rank. The standard methods:
   - **Result randomization**: in a small fraction of traffic, randomly shuffle the top-K results. Then click probability differences across positions are purely position-driven (since random shuffling makes relevance uncorrelated with rank). The propensity at rank k is the click rate at rank k in the random arm divided by the click rate at rank 1.
   - **Intervention harvesting / EM-based methods**: when randomization isn't possible, use observational methods like the Click Chain Model or PBM with EM. Less reliable but doesn't require dedicated traffic.

2. **Compute IPW-corrected label** for each (query, doc) pair:
   ```
   label(q, d) = Σ over impressions of (q, d) at rank k: click / propensity[k]
   ```
   Normalize across (q, d) pairs to get graded labels.

3. **Smooth and clip**. Raw IPW estimates have high variance because 1/p[k] for k=10 is large (small denominator). Cap weights at some maximum (e.g., 10x), or use self-normalized IPW.

4. **Convert to graded labels**. Bucket the corrected scores into 0-4 bins, either by quantile within each query or by absolute thresholds calibrated against human-rated samples.

Let me build this end-to-end with code you can adapt.

**Step 1: the intuition**

A click is the joint event "user examined the doc AND found it relevant":

```
P(click | q, d, k) = P(examined | k) · P(relevant | q, d)
```

P(examined | k) — the *propensity* — depends only on rank k under the position-based model. We want P(relevant | q, d), which is what we'd label. Solving:

```
P(relevant | q, d) = P(click | q, d, k) / P(examined | k)
```

For each click, weight by `1 / P(examined | k)`. Sum and normalize.

**Step 2: estimating P(examined | k)**

*Method A: randomization (cleanest)*

In a small slice of traffic (say 1% of searches), shuffle the top-10 results randomly before showing them. Now for any document, its rank is independent of its relevance. The click rate at rank k in this slice is purely a function of P(examined | k):

```python
from collections import defaultdict

def estimate_propensity_from_random(random_log) -> dict[int, float]:
    """random_log is a list of (rank, clicked) tuples from the randomized slice."""
    impressions = defaultdict(int)
    clicks = defaultdict(int)
    for rank, clicked in random_log:
        impressions[rank] += 1
        clicks[rank] += int(clicked)
    # raw click rate per rank
    rate = {k: clicks[k] / impressions[k] for k in impressions if impressions[k] > 0}
    # normalize so propensity at rank 1 is 1.0 (relative propensity)
    rate_at_1 = rate[1]
    return {k: rate[k] / rate_at_1 for k in rate}
```

Typical output for top 10 looks like `{1: 1.0, 2: 0.65, 3: 0.45, 4: 0.32, 5: 0.24, ...}`. Below rank 5, propensity drops to ~0.1-0.2.

The randomization arm doesn't need to be big — 50K-100K random impressions per rank is enough. But it does mean serving worse results to a small slice of users for the duration; consider a one-week experiment with the smallest slice that gives you statistical power.

*Method B: EM with PBM (when you can't randomize)*

Fit a Position-Based Model with expectation-maximization:

```python
# Using PyClick or similar
from pyclick.click_models.PBM import PBM
from pyclick.utils.YandexRelPredChallengeParser import YandexRelPredChallengeParser

model = PBM()
model.train(sessions)  # list of (query, list_of_(doc, rank, clicked))
examine_probs = {k: model.examine_prob[k] for k in range(1, 11)}
```

Less reliable than randomization (the EM solution has identifiability issues — propensity and relevance can trade off if not regularized) but doesn't require dedicated traffic. Validate by spot-checking against human-rated queries.

**Step 3: compute IPW-corrected labels**

```python
from collections import defaultdict
import math

def ipw_labels(
    click_log: list[tuple[str, str, int, int]],
    propensity: dict[int, float],
    weight_cap: float = 10.0,
    smoothing: float = 0.5,
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], float]:
    """
    click_log: (query_id, doc_id, rank, clicked) per impression.
    Returns a dict mapping (query_id, doc_id) -> corrected relevance score.
    """
    weighted_clicks = defaultdict(float)
    weighted_impressions = defaultdict(float)

    for q, d, rank, clicked in click_log:
        if rank not in propensity:
            continue
        # cap inverse propensity to bound variance
        w = min(1.0 / propensity[rank], weight_cap)
        weighted_impressions[(q, d)] += w
        if clicked:
            weighted_clicks[(q, d)] += w

    # Self-normalized IPW with Laplace-style smoothing
    labels = {}
    for key, imp_w in weighted_impressions.items():
        click_w = weighted_clicks.get(key, 0.0)
        labels[key] = (click_w + smoothing) / (imp_w + 2 * smoothing)
    return labels
```

A few things in this code worth pointing out:

- `weight_cap=10.0`: at rank 10, propensity might be ~0.1 so 1/p = 10. Below that we'd cap. This trades a tiny bias for much lower variance.
- `smoothing=0.5`: a (q, d) pair with 1 impression and 1 click would otherwise get raw label 1.0 — the smoothing pulls low-evidence pairs toward 0.5 so they don't dominate.
- Self-normalized form: dividing by `weighted_impressions` instead of impression count makes the estimator stable when click rates are low.

**Step 4: convert to graded labels**

The IPW score is in [0, 1]. To convert to 0-4 graded labels for NDCG, bucket by per-query quantile or by absolute thresholds:

```python
from collections import defaultdict
import numpy as np

def to_graded(
    ipw_scores: dict[tuple[str, str], float], min_impressions: int = 10
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], int]:
    by_query = defaultdict(list)
    for (q, d), s in ipw_scores.items():
        by_query[q].append((d, s))

    graded = {}
    for q, items in by_query.items():
        if len(items) < 5:
            continue
        scores = np.array([s for _, s in items])
        # bucket by quintile within query
        thresholds = np.quantile(scores, [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
        for d, s in items:
            graded[(q, d)] = int(np.searchsorted(thresholds, s))
    return graded
```

This quintile-within-query approach controls for query-level base rates (some queries are clickier than others). The downside is that even an irrelevant ranking has a label-4 doc per query — calibrate against a human-rated subset to see if the buckets actually correspond to relevance grades.

**Step 5: gotchas**

1. **Position bias isn't the only bias.** Selection bias is bigger: you only have clicks on docs the previous ranker showed. A great doc that's never been retrieved has no label. Mix in random retrieval (not just random ranking) periodically, or accept that your eval set is biased toward what your current system can find.

2. **Trust bias / vertical bias.** Users click brand-name results more, click images more than text snippets. PBM with rank alone misses these. Models like the Cascade Click Model or User Browsing Model handle some of this.

3. **Don't IPW-correct the labels you train your ranker on AND your eval set with the same propensities.** Especially if propensities are estimated from logs the ranker generated. Use a separate held-out propensity estimation arm.

4. **Validate against human ratings.** Pull 200 (q, d) pairs spanning your label range, have humans rate them, compute correlation between human grade and IPW grade. If correlation is below ~0.6, your propensity model is off — check for trust bias or selection effects.

5. **Refresh propensities.** UI changes (different snippet design, new image carousels) change examination probabilities. Re-estimate quarterly or whenever the SERP layout meaningfully changes.

This is the core machinery. The honest version: most teams ship a much rougher cut (binary clicks with capped weights, no full PBM) and it's still better than uncorrected clicks. Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good — get the basic IPW pipeline running, validate with a small human-rated set, iterate.
