**Why path compression and rollback are incompatible.** The α(n) bound for union-find depends on path compression as an amortized argument: a single find can be O(n) in the worst case, but its compression "prepays" for future finds, amortizing down to α(n). When you rollback, you erase those prepayments — the future operations that would have benefited never happen, but the compression's cost was already paid. So rollback breaks the amortized analysis: undoing a sequence of m compressing operations and re-running them gives you O(m·n) in the worst case, not O(m·α(n)).

There's also a mechanical issue: each find can rewrite many parent pointers, so logging changes for rollback costs O(path length) per find — exactly the savings compression buys you.

2. **Link-cut trees as a connectivity structure.** Forest of splay trees, O(log n) amortized per op. Supports `link`, `cut`, `find_root`, so it natively handles edge removal. def find(self, x: int) -> int:
```python
    # Path halving: faster than no-compression on average,
    # still O(log n) worst-case, fully rollbackable since we log changes.
    while self.parent[x] != x:
        gp = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
        if gp != self.parent[x]:
            self.history.append(('halve', x, self.parent[x]))
            self.parent[x] = gp
        x = gp
    return x
```

**Skeleton**

```ts
interface Shape {
  id: string;
  x: number;
  y: number;
  width: number;
  height: number;
  fill: string;
}

interface Doc {
  shapes: Record<string, Shape>;
  order: string[];
}

// A Command knows how to apply itself and produce its inverse given the pre-state.
interface Command {
  readonly type: string;
  apply(doc: Doc): Doc;
  invert(preState: Doc): Command;
}

class MoveShapes implements Command {
  readonly type = 'move';
  constructor(private ids: string[], private dx: number, private dy: number) {}
  apply(doc: Doc): Doc {
    const shapes = { ...doc.shapes };
    for (const id of this.ids) {
      const s = shapes[id];
      if (s) shapes[id] = { ...s, x: s.x + this.dx, y: s.y + this.dy };
    }
    return { ...doc, shapes };
  }
  invert(): Command {
    return new MoveShapes(this.ids, -this.dx, -this.dy);
  }
  // Coalesce with a continuing drag of the same selection.
  tryMerge(other: Command): Command | null {
    if (other instanceof MoveShapes && sameSet(this.ids, other.ids)) {
      return new MoveShapes(this.ids, this.dx + other.dx, this.dy + other.dy);
    }
    return null;
  }
}

class DeleteShapes implements Command {
  readonly type = 'delete';
  constructor(private ids: string[]) {}
  apply(doc: Doc): Doc {
    const shapes = { ...doc.shapes };
    for (const id of this.ids) delete shapes[id];
    return { ...doc, shapes, order: doc.order.filter((id) => !this.ids.includes(id)) };
  }
  invert(preState: Doc): Command {
    // Inverse must capture the deleted shapes' data.
    const captured = this.ids
      .map((id) => ({ id, shape: preState.shapes[id], index: preState.order.indexOf(id) }))
      .filter((x) => x.shape);
    return new RestoreShapes(captured);
  }
}

class RestoreShapes implements Command {
  readonly type = 'restore';
  constructor(private entries: { id: string; shape: Shape; index: number }[]) {}
  apply(doc: Doc): Doc {
    const shapes = { ...doc.shapes };
    const order = [...doc.order];
    for (const { id, shape, index } of this.entries) {
      shapes[id] = shape;
      order.splice(Math.min(index, order.length), 0, id);
    }
    return { ...doc, shapes, order };
  }
  invert(): Command {
    return new DeleteShapes(this.entries.map((e) => e.id));
  }
}

function sameSet(a: string[], b: string[]): boolean {
  if (a.length !== b.length) return false;
  const s = new Set(a);
  return b.every((x) => s.has(x));
}
```

**The history controller with coalescing**

```ts
interface HistoryEntry {
  command: Command;
  inverse: Command;
}

class History {
  private past: HistoryEntry[] = [];
  private future: HistoryEntry[] = [];
  private readonly maxDepth = 500;

  execute(doc: Doc, command: Command, coalesce = false): Doc {
    const inverse = command.invert(doc);
    const next = command.apply(doc);

    if (coalesce && this.past.length > 0) {
      const top = this.past[this.past.length - 1];
      const merged = (top.command as any).tryMerge?.(command);
      if (merged) {
        // Keep the older inverse (undoes back to pre-drag start), replace forward op.
        this.past[this.past.length - 1] = { command: merged, inverse: top.inverse };
        this.future = [];
        return next;
      }
    }

    this.past.push({ command, inverse });
    if (this.past.length > this.maxDepth) this.past.shift();
    this.future = [];
    return next;
  }

  undo(doc: Doc): Doc {
    const entry = this.past.pop();
    if (!entry) return doc;
    this.future.push(entry);
    return entry.inverse.apply(doc);
  }

  redo(doc: Doc): Doc {
    const entry = this.future.pop();
    if (!entry) return doc;
    this.past.push(entry);
    return entry.command.apply(doc);
  }
}
```

A drag calls `execute(doc, new MoveShapes(ids, dx, dy), /*coalesce=*/ true)` on every mousemove. They merge into a single history entry. On mouseup, call once more with `coalesce = false` to seal the entry so the next action doesn't fold into it.

Good instinct. Here are three more aggregation traps, each with a real example.

**The ecological fallacy**

Countries with higher average chocolate consumption win more Nobel Prizes (real correlation, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2012). Conclusion: eat more chocolate to become a genius?

Obviously not. The correlation exists at the country level but tells you nothing about individuals. Rich countries consume more chocolate AND fund more research. The ecological fallacy is assuming that group-level correlations hold at the individual level.

**The Will Rogers phenomenon**

Named after Will Rogers' quip: "When the Okies left Oklahoma and moved to California, they raised the average intelligence level in both states."

This happens in medicine with cancer staging. When diagnostic technology improves, some patients previously classified as Stage 1 (good prognosis) get reclassified as Stage 2 (worse prognosis). These patients are the worst of Stage 1 and the best of Stage 2. Removing them from Stage 1 raises Stage 1's survival rate. Adding them to Stage 2 raises Stage 2's survival rate. Both stages show improvement — even if no treatment changed. This is called "stage migration" and has led to false claims of therapeutic progress.

**Survivorship bias**

During World War II, the military examined bombers returning from missions and found bullet holes concentrated on the fuselage and wings. Initial recommendation: add armor to these areas. Abraham Wald pointed out the error: the planes they were examining were the ones that survived. The holes showed where a plane COULD be hit and still return. The missing bullet holes — on engines and cockpits — were on the planes that didn't come back. Armor should go where the returning planes WEREN'T hit.

**The common thread**

All of these — Simpson's paradox, ecological fallacy, Will Rogers, survivorship bias — are failures to ask: "What data am I NOT seeing, and how would it change my conclusion?" The aggregated data you see is always a summary, and the summarization process can destroy the signal. Always ask what was averaged over, what was excluded, and whether subgroups tell a different story.

You're spotting something real, and clearing it up is the whole point of understanding the proof. Euclid's argument does **not** claim that N is prime. It claims something weaker but sufficient: N has at least one prime factor that isn't in the list {p1, p2, ..., pn}.

Here is the core mechanical fact the proof uses. Suppose some prime p divides N. Then since

    N = p1 * p2 * ... * pn + 1,

if p were equal to one of the pi, then p would divide both N and p1*p2*...*pn. So p would divide their difference:

    N - (p1*p2*...*pn) = 1.

Now the reason your intuition balked: you're right that N can be composite. In fact, it usually is. Take the small list {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13} and form

    N = 2 * 3 * 5 * 7 * 11 * 13 + 1 = 30031.

You might guess 30031 is prime. It isn't. Factoring gives

    30031 = 59 * 509.

Both 59 and 509 are prime. Neither is in our starting list. So N is composite, but its prime factorization exposes two new primes. That's exactly what the proof promises: the act of factoring N (which is guaranteed to terminate because N > 1) must produce at least one prime outside the original list.

So the logical structure is:

1. Suppose, for contradiction, that the primes are exactly p1, p2, ..., pn — a complete finite list.
2. Form N = p1 * p2 * ... * pn + 1. Note N > 1.
3. N has a prime factor p (every integer greater than 1 does — fundamental theorem of arithmetic).
4. That p cannot be any pi, by the divisibility argument above.
5. So p is a prime outside the list. But we assumed the list was complete. Contradiction.
6. Therefore the list of primes cannot be finite.

The thing you were implicitly worried about — "what if N is composite with weird factors" — isn't a problem, it's the generic case. The proof is robust to that because it only needs *some* prime factor, and any prime factor will do.

The cleaner modern phrasing is: "N has a prime divisor, and that divisor is not in the list." Once that's the version in your head, the argument becomes airtight and, I'd say, beautiful — it extracts a new prime from any finite list, mechanically, forever.

Yes, with a caveat: full SoA is one option, but the simpler **hot/cold split** often gets you most of the win without restructuring everything.

First the math. Your `struct Particle` is roughly 40-48 bytes after padding (3 floats pos + 3 floats vel + float mass + 32-bit color + float age + 32-bit flags). The physics step touches 24 bytes (pos + vel) per particle but pulls a full 48-byte struct into L1 each time — you're using 50% of the bytes you fetch. At 500K particles = ~24 MB, well past any per-core LLC slice, so the physics step is moving 24 MB through DRAM when it only needs 12 MB worth of useful data.

**Option 1: hot/cold split.** Keep the fields physics needs together; move the rest into a cold struct.

```cpp
struct ParticleHot {   // 32 bytes — half a cacheline
    float pos[3];
    float vel[3];
    float mass;
    std::uint32_t flags;
};
struct ParticleCold {  // 12 bytes
    std::uint32_t color;
    float age;
    float pad;         // or another field
};

std::vector<ParticleHot>  hot;
std::vector<ParticleCold> cold;
```

Now the physics pass scans `hot` linearly: 32 bytes/particle, all relevant. DRAM traffic drops from 24 MB to 16 MB and bandwidth utilization goes from 50% to 100%. For a bandwidth-bound kernel, this is roughly a 1.5x speedup — the math is simple bytes-moved.

The render pass reads `pos` from `hot` and `color` from `cold`. Two streams, both sequential, both prefetched well by the hardware prefetcher. Total bytes read per particle: 12 (pos) + 4 (color) = 16 vs the original 16 you'd want — same bandwidth efficiency as full SoA for render.

**Option 2: full SoA.**

```cpp
struct Particles {
    std::vector<float> px, py, pz;
    std::vector<float> vx, vy, vz;
    std::vector<float> mass;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> color;
    std::vector<float> age;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> flags;
};
```

Maximum bandwidth efficiency on every pass — physics reads 6 contiguous arrays (24 B/particle, all useful). Render reads 4 arrays (px, py, pz, color, 16 B/particle, all useful). Also the natural form for SIMD: each array is just a flat float stream you can `_mm512_loadu_ps` 16 lanes at a time.

The cost: more arrays to keep in sync on insert/delete. Function signatures get awkward — you can't pass a single particle by reference; you pass `(arrays, index)`. If you have generic algorithms that take a particle, refactoring is painful.

**My recommendation for your case**: start with the hot/cold split. It's a 30-minute change, gives you most of the bandwidth win, and physics + render code barely changes (just one extra struct member access). Move to full SoA if (a) you want to vectorize physics with SIMD, or (b) the hot/cold version is still bandwidth-bound and you need every byte.

LLC-load-misses should drop by ~30% with hot/cold, ~50% with full SoA, on the physics pass. If they don't, you've found a different bottleneck and the layout change won't help.

For a Verlet integrator that streams over every particle every frame, pure SoA is the right call — and yes, there's a hybrid (AoSoA) but it doesn't help here. Let me show why.

**SoA Verlet with AVX-512:**

```cpp
void verlet_step(Particles& p, std::size_t n, float dt) {
    const __m512 vdt = _mm512_set1_ps(dt);
    std::size_t i = 0;
    for (; i + 16 <= n; i += 16) {
        __m512 px = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.px[i]);
        __m512 py = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.py[i]);
        __m512 pz = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.pz[i]);
        __m512 vx = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.vx[i]);
        __m512 vy = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.vy[i]);
        __m512 vz = _mm512_loadu_ps(&p.vz[i]);

        // Apply forces (gravity on y, say).
        vy = _mm512_fmadd_ps(_mm512_set1_ps(-9.81f), vdt, vy);

        // Integrate position.
        px = _mm512_fmadd_ps(vx, vdt, px);
        py = _mm512_fmadd_ps(vy, vdt, py);
        pz = _mm512_fmadd_ps(vz, vdt, pz);

        _mm512_storeu_ps(&p.px[i], px);
        _mm512_storeu_ps(&p.py[i], py);
        _mm512_storeu_ps(&p.pz[i], pz);
        _mm512_storeu_ps(&p.vy[i], vy);  // only vy changed
    }
    // Masked tail or scalar epilogue.
}
```

Notice how clean this is: each load is a contiguous block of 16 floats. The hardware prefetcher sees 6 forward streams (px, py, pz, vx, vy, vz) — well within its capacity (~16 streams on Intel, ~8-12 on Apple/Arm). All the arithmetic is uniform across SIMD lanes.

You could honestly drop the intrinsics and write the scalar loop with `#pragma omp simd` or just `-O3` — Clang and GCC both autovectorize this perfectly because SoA is the layout autovectorizers love. Pure SoA + simple scalar code is often the right starting point; reach for intrinsics only when you need to fine-tune.

**AoSoA — when it does pay.** AoSoA is an array of structs, where each struct holds fixed-size arrays of each field. With tile size matching SIMD width (16 here):

```cpp
struct ParticleTile {
    alignas(64) float px[16], py[16], pz[16];
    alignas(64) float vx[16], vy[16], vz[16];
};
std::vector<ParticleTile> tiles;  // ceil(n/16) tiles
```

For your Verlet step, AoSoA is essentially identical performance to SoA — same SIMD code, same memory traffic. No reason to prefer it.

AoSoA earns its complexity when you have access patterns that touch *all fields of a subset of particles*: ray-hit tests, neighbor queries, picking. In SoA, fetching 'all fields for particle 5000' means hitting 6 different cachelines, each ~80% wasted (you take one float per line). In AoSoA, particle 5000 lives in tile 312, and that tile's 6 fields are within 6 contiguous cachelines — much better when you're going to touch all of them. It also matters for GPU streaming where you want chunked, predictable transfer units.

For a per-frame Verlet integrator over every particle, you don't have those access patterns. Pure SoA is simpler and equally fast.

**One last thing to verify.** Make sure your `std::vector<float>` allocations are 64-byte aligned. The default allocator gives you 16-byte alignment on most platforms, which is enough for `loadu` (unaligned load is free on Zen 4 / Ice Lake+ when it happens to be aligned). But for *stores* and for non-temporal hints, true 64-byte alignment matters. Either use `boost::alignment::aligned_allocator`, `std::aligned_alloc` + manual vector emulation, or `std::vector<float, AlignedAllocator<float, 64>>`. C++17's `std::pmr` with an aligned upstream resource also works. Verify with:

```cpp
assert(reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p.px.data()) % 64 == 0);
```

If you're at 16-byte alignment that crosses a cacheline, individual SIMD loads can split across two cachelines — measurable on Zen 4 (~5% hit) but rarely catastrophic.

Creating a database connection is expensive (~20-100ms for TCP handshake + authentication + SSL). A connection pool maintains a cache of open connections that can be reused.

```python
# Without pooling: new connection per request
async def handle_request():
    conn = await asyncpg.connect(dsn)  # 50ms
    result = await conn.fetch(query)    # 5ms
    await conn.close()                  # 10ms
    # Total: 65ms, connection overhead dominates

# With pooling: reuse existing connection
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(dsn, min_size=5, max_size=20)
async def handle_request():
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:  # <1ms (already connected)
        result = await conn.fetch(query) # 5ms
    # Total: ~6ms, 10x faster
```

**Key parameters:**
- `min_size`: connections kept open when idle
- `max_size`: maximum concurrent connections (match your database's `max_connections`)
- `max_idle_time`: close idle connections after this duration
- `max_lifetime`: close connections after this total lifetime (prevents stale connections)

**Common mistake:** Setting max_size too high. PostgreSQL handles ~100-300 connections well. More causes contention. If you need more concurrent requests than connections, use PgBouncer (a connection multiplexer) in front of PostgreSQL.

At 500 jobs/minute, a hand-rolled Redis queue is the right call. The core is about 100 lines of Python. The trick is handling worker crashes without losing jobs.

**The architecture:**

```
Producer -> [pending queue] -> Worker -> [processing:{worker_id}] -> done
                                                    |
                                              crash recovery
                                              (requeue after timeout)
```

```python
import json
import time
import uuid
import signal
import redis
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict
from typing import Callable


@dataclass
class Job:
    task: str
    payload: dict
    job_id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: str(uuid.uuid4()))
    enqueued_at: float = field(default_factory=time.time)
    attempts: int = 0

    def serialize(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps(asdict(self))

    @classmethod
    def deserialize(cls, data: str) -> 'Job':
        return cls(**json.loads(data))


class JobQueue:
    def __init__(
        self,
        client: redis.Redis,
        queue_name: str = "jobs:pending",
        max_retries: int = 3,
        visibility_timeout: int = 300,  # 5 minutes
    ) -> None:
        self.client = client
        self.queue_name = queue_name
        self.max_retries = max_retries
        self.visibility_timeout = visibility_timeout

    def enqueue(self, task: str, payload: dict) -> str:
        job = Job(task=task, payload=payload)
        self.client.lpush(self.queue_name, job.serialize())
        return job.job_id

    def _processing_key(self, worker_id: str) -> str:
        return f"jobs:processing:{worker_id}"

    def dequeue(self, worker_id: str, timeout: int = 5) -> Job | None:
        """Atomically move a job from pending to this worker's processing list."""
        result = self.client.blmove(
            self.queue_name,
            self._processing_key(worker_id),
            timeout,
            "RIGHT",  # pop from right of pending
            "LEFT",   # push to left of processing
        )
        if result is None:
            return None
        return Job.deserialize(result)

    def complete(self, worker_id: str, job: Job) -> None:
        """Remove job from processing list."""
        self.client.lrem(self._processing_key(worker_id), 1, job.serialize())

    def fail(self, worker_id: str, job: Job) -> None:
        """Retry or move to dead letter queue."""
        self.client.lrem(self._processing_key(worker_id), 1, job.serialize())
        job.attempts += 1
        if job.attempts < self.max_retries:
            self.client.lpush(self.queue_name, job.serialize())
        else:
            self.client.lpush("jobs:dead", job.serialize())
```

```python
        self.handlers = handlers
        self.worker_id = f"worker-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"
        self._running = True

        signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, self._shutdown)
        signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, self._shutdown)
```

```python
WORKER_REGISTRY = "workers:active"


class Worker:
    def run(self) -> None:
        # Register on startup
        self.queue.client.sadd(WORKER_REGISTRY, self.worker_id)

        heartbeat = threading.Thread(target=self._heartbeat_loop, daemon=True)
        heartbeat.start()

        try:
            while self._running:
                job = self.queue.dequeue(self.worker_id)
                if job is None:
                    continue
                # ... process job
        finally:
            # Unregister on clean shutdown
            self.queue.client.srem(WORKER_REGISTRY, self.worker_id)
            self.queue.client.delete(f"workers:heartbeat:{self.worker_id}")

    requeued = 0
    worker_ids = client.smembers(WORKER_REGISTRY)  # O(n) where n = worker count, not keyspace

    for worker_id in worker_ids:
        wid = worker_id if isinstance(worker_id, str) else worker_id.decode()
        heartbeat_key = f"workers:heartbeat:{wid}"
        processing_key = f"jobs:processing:{wid}"

        if client.exists(heartbeat_key):
            continue

        # Dead worker — requeue jobs and remove from registry
        while True:
            job_data = client.rpop(processing_key)
            if job_data is None:
                break
            job = Job.deserialize(job_data)
            job.attempts += 1
            if job.attempts < 3:
                client.lpush(queue_name, job.serialize())
                requeued += 1
            else:
                client.lpush("jobs:dead", job.serialize())

        client.srem(WORKER_REGISTRY, wid)
        print(f"Removed dead worker {wid}, requeued {requeued} jobs")

    return requeued
```

`SMEMBERS` on a set of 10-50 worker IDs is O(n) where n is the number of workers, not the number of keys in Redis. It completes in microseconds regardless of how large your Redis instance is.

Write a Python context manager that provides database transaction semantics — commit on success, rollback on exception, with savepoint support for nesting.

<think>

So the context manager needs to track depth: the outermost `with transaction(conn):` does BEGIN/COMMIT, and inner ones use SAVEPOINT/RELEASE SAVEPOINT (or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT on failure). I'll use a connection wrapper or track nesting depth on the connection object. Here's a transaction context manager that handles nesting via savepoints, with clean commit/rollback semantics.

```python
"""Transaction context manager with savepoint-based nesting."""
import sqlite3
from contextlib import contextmanager


class TransactionManager:
    """Wraps a DB connection to provide nested transaction support via savepoints."""

    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn
        self._depth = 0
        # Disable sqlite3's auto-transaction so we control BEGIN/COMMIT
        self.conn.isolation_level = None

    @contextmanager
    def transaction(self):
        """Context manager: BEGIN/COMMIT at top level, SAVEPOINT/RELEASE when nested."""
        self._depth += 1
        is_outermost = self._depth == 1
        savepoint_name = f"sp_{self._depth}"

        try:
            if is_outermost:
                self.conn.execute("BEGIN")
            else:
                self.conn.execute(f"SAVEPOINT {savepoint_name}")

            yield self.conn

            if is_outermost:
                self.conn.execute("COMMIT")
            else:
                self.conn.execute(f"RELEASE SAVEPOINT {savepoint_name}")

        except Exception:
            if is_outermost:
                self.conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
            else:
                self.conn.execute(f"ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT {savepoint_name}")
            raise

        finally:
            self._depth -= 1


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Usage example
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    tm = TransactionManager(conn)

    # Setup
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT, balance INTEGER)")
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('alice', 1000)")
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('bob', 500)")

    # --- Successful nested transaction ---
    with tm.transaction() as c:
        c.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 200 WHERE name = 'alice'")

        with tm.transaction() as c2:
            c2.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 200 WHERE name = 'bob'")
        # Inner savepoint released, both updates will commit together

    rows = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY name").fetchall()
    print("After transfer:", rows)
    # [('alice', 800), ('bob', 700)]

    # --- Inner failure, outer survives ---
    with tm.transaction() as c:
        c.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE name = 'alice'")

        try:
            with tm.transaction() as c2:
                c2.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE name = 'bob'")
                raise ValueError("Simulated inner failure")
        except ValueError:
            pass  # Inner rolled back to savepoint, outer continues

        # Alice's deduction is still pending in the outer transaction
        c.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE name = 'alice'")
        # Undo alice's deduction since bob's credit failed

    rows = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY name").fetchall()
    print("After failed inner:", rows)
    # [('alice', 800), ('bob', 700)] -- unchanged, as expected

    # --- Outer failure rolls back everything ---
    try:
        with tm.transaction() as c:
            c.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE name = 'alice'")

            with tm.transaction() as c2:
                c2.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = 9999 WHERE name = 'bob'")

            raise RuntimeError("Outer transaction fails")
    except RuntimeError:
        pass

    rows = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY name").fetchall()
    print("After outer failure:", rows)
    # [('alice', 800), ('bob', 700)] -- everything rolled back

    conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## How Nesting Works

The core idea is depth tracking. The first call to `transaction()` issues `BEGIN` and the last (outermost) exit issues `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. Every nested call uses savepoints instead:

```
with transaction():          # depth 1 -> BEGIN
    with transaction():      # depth 2 -> SAVEPOINT sp_2
        with transaction():  # depth 3 -> SAVEPOINT sp_3
        # success            # RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp_3
    # success                # RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp_2
# success                    # COMMIT
```

When an inner block raises, only its savepoint is rolled back. The outer transaction can catch the exception and continue, or let it propagate (which rolls back everything when it hits the outermost block).

## Production Considerations

For real use, you'd want to add: (1) a `read_only` flag that uses `BEGIN READONLY` where supported, (2) a configurable isolation level, and (3) thread-local depth tracking if your connection pool shares connections across threads. Libraries like SQLAlchemy's `Session.begin_nested()` use this exact same savepoint pattern internally.

`useMemo` caches a **value**. `useCallback` caches a **function**.

```jsx
// useMemo — expensive computation
const sorted = useMemo(() => {
  return items.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
}, [items]);

// useCallback — stable function reference
const handleClick = useCallback((id) => {
  setSelected(id);
}, []); // Same function object across renders
```

**`useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.**

**When to use:**
- `useMemo`: Expensive calculations that shouldn't re-run on every render
- `useCallback`: Functions passed as props to `memo()`-wrapped children, or as dependencies of other hooks

**When NOT to use:**
```jsx
// Don't memoize cheap operations
const fullName = useMemo(() => `${first} ${last}`, [first, last]); // Overkill
const fullName = `${first} ${last}`; // Just compute it

// Don't memoize unless a child actually uses React.memo
const handleClick = useCallback(() => {}, []); // Useless if Child isn't memoized
```

Rule: Don't optimize until you measure. Most React performance issues are structural (too many components re-rendering), not computational.

An index is a data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the entire table.

**How a B-tree index works:**
Imagine a phone book. To find "Smith," you don't read every page — you use alphabetical ordering to jump close to "S," then narrow down. A B-tree works the same way with your data.

The index stores sorted copies of the indexed column(s), each pointing to the full row on disk. A query like `WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'` traverses the tree (O(log n) comparisons) instead of scanning every row (O(n)).

**Types of indexes:**

| Type | Use case | Example |
|------|----------|----------|
| B-tree (default) | Equality and range queries | `WHERE age > 25 AND age < 50` |
| Hash | Equality only, very fast | `WHERE email = 'x@y.com'` |
| GiST | Geometric, full-text search | PostGIS spatial queries |
| GIN | Array containment, JSONB | `WHERE tags @> '{python}'` |
| BRIN | Large sequential data | Time-series data by timestamp |

**Composite indexes — column order matters:**
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders ON orders(customer_id, created_at);

-- Uses the index (leftmost prefix match):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- Does NOT use the index (no leftmost column):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';
```

**When NOT to index:**
- Columns with very low cardinality (boolean columns with 50/50 distribution)
- Tables with fewer than ~1000 rows (full scan is faster)
- Write-heavy tables where index maintenance outweighs read benefit
- Columns rarely used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses

**Index overhead:** Every index slows writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE must update the index) and uses disk space. Don't add indexes speculatively — add them based on measured query performance.

Plan the response:

The mechanical definition hides a really clean picture. Let me rebuild the intuition.

**Distributions as row vectors.**

Suppose your chain has states {1, 2, ..., n}. A probability distribution at time t is

    pi_t = [pi_t(1), pi_t(2), ..., pi_t(n)]

where pi_t(i) is the probability of being in state i at time t, and the entries sum to 1. Picture it as a *mass distribution*: pi_t(i) units of probability-mass sitting on state i.

**The transition matrix as a flow operator.**

The matrix P has entries P[i, j] = P(next state = j | current state = i). Each row of P is itself a distribution (sums to 1). What happens in one step?

The probability of being at state j at time t+1 is the total mass flowing *into* j, summed over all possible previous states:

    pi_{t+1}(j) = sum over i of pi_t(i) * P[i, j].

That's precisely the matrix product pi_t * P (treating pi_t as a row vector). So **left multiplication by P is literally "run the chain one step."**

**Stationary = fixed point of evolution.**

A stationary distribution pi is one that doesn't change under evolution: pi * P = pi. Rewrite as pi * P = 1 * pi — this is an eigenvalue equation with eigenvalue 1. Hence "left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1." The word "left" is just bookkeeping about which side we multiply; the *meaning* is "distribution that evolves into itself."

**Why eigenvalue 1 always exists.**

Every stochastic matrix P (rows sum to 1) has the all-ones column vector as a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1:

    P * [1,1,...,1]^T = [1,1,...,1]^T   (because each row sums to 1).

Since P and P^T have the same eigenvalues, 1 is also a left eigenvalue. By Perron-Frobenius (applied to irreducible non-negative matrices), for an irreducible chain there is a *unique* left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1, up to scaling, and it has strictly positive entries. Normalizing it to sum to 1 gives the unique stationary distribution.

**Worked example: 2-state chain.**

Let

    P = [[0.8, 0.2],
         [0.5, 0.5]]

(From state 1, stay with prob 0.8; from state 2, stay with prob 0.5.)

Method A — eigenvector:

Solve pi * P = pi with pi = [a, b]:
    a = 0.8a + 0.5b  ->  0.2a = 0.5b  ->  a = 2.5 b.

With a + b = 1: a = 5/7, b = 2/7. So pi = [5/7, 2/7].

Method B — flow balance (the physical argument):

In equilibrium, flow from 1 to 2 must equal flow from 2 to 1:

    a * P[1,2] = b * P[2,1]
    a * 0.2 = b * 0.5.

Same equation. This is the **detailed balance** view, and it's the same fact dressed differently: mass conservation at each state in steady state.

For chains that satisfy detailed balance (reversible chains), Method B is often faster because you get one equation per edge rather than solving a linear system.

**Why this matters operationally.**

Once you think of P as evolving distributions, the spectral decomposition of P tells you *how fast* pi_t -> pi. If the eigenvalues of P are 1 = lambda_1 > |lambda_2| >= |lambda_3| >= ..., then

    pi_t - pi  ~  (const) * lambda_2^t

for large t. The **spectral gap** 1 - |lambda_2| is what controls mixing time. The stationary eigenvector tells you *where* you end up; the second eigenvector and its eigenvalue tell you *how fast* you get there.

So the "left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1" framing isn't just convention — it's the fixed-point view of a linear dynamical system, and it plugs directly into the bigger machinery (spectral gap, mixing times, MCMC convergence, Cheeger inequalities). Once you have it, the other eigenvalues become meaningful objects too.

`npm ci` deletes `node_modules` before extracting. So if you're caching `node_modules` and running `npm ci`, the cache hit is genuine — and then the very next step throws everything away. The cache reports success because it restored what you asked for; the install is slow because it's still hitting the npm registry for every package.

Fix: cache the **npm download cache** at `~/.npm`, not `node_modules`. Then `npm ci` extracts from the local cache instead of downloading.

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: '20'
    cache: 'npm'  # built-in: caches ~/.npm keyed on package-lock.json

- run: npm ci
```

The `cache: 'npm'` option in `setup-node` does the right thing automatically. If you're using a manual `actions/cache` step, here's what it should look like:

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-node-
```

Key rules to internalize:

- **Hash the lockfile, not the source files.** Source files change on every commit; the lockfile only changes when dependencies change. Hashing source files means a cache miss every commit, which is why some teams "have a cache" that effectively never hits.

**Layer ordering** — the canonical "deps before source" pattern, but done correctly:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app

# Copy ONLY the files that determine deps. Lockfile + manifest, nothing else.
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# BuildKit cache mount: ~/.npm persists across builds, NOT in image.
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit

FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

Key points:

- The `COPY package.json package-lock.json ./` only invalidates when those two files change. If your team adds a typo fix to a TS file, the deps stage stays cached, and `npm ci` is skipped entirely.
- `--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm` is BuildKit's persistent cache. Even when the lockfile *does* change and `npm ci` re-runs, it pulls tarballs from the cached `~/.npm` rather than the network. This is the in-Docker equivalent of the GHA cache fix you just did. **The cache mount is not in the final image** — no bloat.
- Multi-stage with `deps`/`build`/`runtime` keeps the runtime image small and ensures dev deps don't ship to prod.

For other ecosystems:

```dockerfile
# Go
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    go build -o /app/server ./cmd/server

# Rust
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/usr/local/cargo/registry \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/app/target \
    cargo build --release

# Python (pip)
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**Multi-arch**: this is where most teams' builds slow down 5-10x and they don't understand why.

The core problem: `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` builds the Dockerfile *twice*, once per arch. Each platform has its own layer cache (a layer is identified by content, and arm64 binaries have different content). If you're on an amd64 GitHub runner, the arm64 build uses QEMU emulation, which is single-threaded and slow — `npm ci` that takes 30 seconds natively can take 8 minutes under QEMU.

1. **Build arch-independent steps once on `BUILDPLATFORM`**, then cross-compile. For Go and Rust this is huge:

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.22 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    go mod download
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

The build stage runs on the *builder's* native arch (`$BUILDPLATFORM` = amd64 on amd64 runners) and produces output for `$TARGETPLATFORM`. Go cross-compiles trivially. Rust does too with the right targets installed. Node and Python with native modules are harder — for those, use native runners.

2. **Use native multi-arch runners** if speed matters. GitHub now offers ARM-hosted runners (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`). Run two parallel jobs, one per arch, each native, then combine into a manifest list:

```yaml
jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - platform: linux/amd64
            runner: ubuntu-24.04
          - platform: linux/arm64
            runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: ${{ matrix.platform }}
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=${{ matrix.platform }}
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=${{ matrix.platform }}
          outputs: type=image,name=ghcr.io/org/app,push-by-digest=true,name-canonical=true,push=true

  manifest:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      # Combine the per-arch digests into a single multi-arch tag.
      # Use docker buildx imagetools create.
      - run: |
          docker buildx imagetools create -t ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }} \
            ghcr.io/org/app@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest-amd64 }} \
            ghcr.io/org/app@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest-arm64 }}
```

Note `scope=${{ matrix.platform }}` on the GHA cache — this is critical. Without it, both jobs write to the same cache key and overwrite each other's layers, giving you ~50% cache hit rate forever.

3. **`type=gha,mode=max`** caches all intermediate layers, not just the final image. Default `mode=min` only caches the layers needed to produce the final image, missing build-stage layers. For multi-stage Dockerfiles, you almost always want `max`.

If you have to stick with QEMU (no native ARM runner budget), at minimum set `cache-to: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/org/app:buildcache,mode=max` so the cache is shared across runs of different commits — losing a QEMU build to cache thrash is far more painful than to a registry round-trip.

What is the strangler fig pattern for migrating legacy systems?

<think>
The strangler fig pattern is a migration strategy named after the actual strangler fig tree that grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it. Martin Fowler coined the term for software migration. The core idea is incremental replacement rather than big-bang rewrite.

The key insight is that this is reversible at every step — if a migrated feature has issues, you can route traffic back to the legacy system.

The strangler fig pattern (Martin Fowler) incrementally replaces a legacy system by routing new functionality through a new system while leaving the old system running.

**How it works:**
1. Add a facade/proxy in front of the legacy system
2. Implement new features in the new system; the facade routes to it
3. Gradually migrate existing features one by one to the new system
4. The facade routes each migrated feature to the new system
5. Eventually, all traffic goes to the new system; remove the legacy

```
[Client] → [Facade/Proxy] → /new-feature → [New System]
                          → /old-feature → [Legacy System]
                          → /migrated    → [New System]
```

**Why it works:** Zero big-bang risk. Each migration is small and reversible. The legacy system remains functional throughout. You can stop at any point and still have a working system.

**Compared to the big rewrite:** Rewrites are high-risk (months of development before any user sees it, high chance of missing requirements, team is maintaining two systems). The strangler pattern delivers value continuously.

```python
from functools import lru_cache
from pydantic import Field, PostgresDsn
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        env_prefix="",  # set to "APP_" if you want APP_DATABASE_URL etc.
        case_sensitive=False,
        extra="ignore",  # ignore unknown env vars rather than error
    )

    database_url: PostgresDsn = Field(alias="DATABASE_URL")
    redis_url: str = Field(alias="REDIS_URL")
    debug: bool = False
    log_level: str = "INFO"
    pool_size: int = 20
    secret_key: str = Field(alias="SECRET_KEY", min_length=32)

@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()
```

Key differences from v1 worth knowing:

- `Field(env="X")` is now `Field(alias="X")`. The `env=` kwarg is gone.
- `Config` inner class is now `model_config = SettingsConfigDict(...)`.
- `case_sensitive` defaults to `False` (matches `DATABASE_URL` to `database_url`).
- Validation errors now raise on instantiation, not lazily.
- `extra="ignore"` is recommended — without it, any extra env var causes a validation error, which is annoying when your container has hundreds of unrelated env vars.

Nested settings work via `__` separator:

```python
class DBSettings(BaseSettings):
    host: str = "localhost"
    port: int = 5432
    pool_size: int = 20

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter="__")
    db: DBSettings = DBSettings()
```

The epsilon-delta definition is the answer to a question. If you haven't heard the question, the answer looks like random symbols. So let me start with the question.

**The question:** What does "f(x) approaches L as x approaches a" actually mean? Informally: "f(x) gets close to L when x gets close to a." But "close" is vague. How close? Close enough for what purpose?

**The game.** Think of it as a challenge between a Skeptic and a Prover.

- **Skeptic**: "I don't believe f(x) truly approaches L. I challenge you: make f(x) within **epsilon = 0.1** of L."
- **Prover**: "Fine. If you keep x within **delta = 0.03** of a, then f(x) will be within 0.1 of L."
- **Skeptic**: "Okay, but what about epsilon = 0.001?"
- **Prover**: "Then use delta = 0.0003."
- **Skeptic**: "Epsilon = 10^(-100)?"
- **Prover**: "Delta = 3.33 * 10^(-101)."

The limit exists if the Prover can win **no matter what epsilon the Skeptic chooses**. That's what "for all epsilon > 0, there exists delta > 0" means — the Prover has a response to every challenge.

**Concrete example:** Prove lim(x -> 2) (3x + 1) = 7.

Sceptic gives epsilon > 0. We need |f(x) - L| < epsilon, meaning |3x + 1 - 7| < epsilon, meaning |3x - 6| < epsilon, meaning 3|x - 2| < epsilon, meaning |x - 2| < epsilon/3.

So the Prover's strategy: set delta = epsilon/3. Whenever |x - 2| < delta = epsilon/3:

|f(x) - 7| = |3x - 6| = 3|x - 2| < 3 * (epsilon/3) = epsilon. Done.

The proof IS the Prover's winning strategy. The "template" you've been following — assume |x - a| < delta, show |f(x) - L| < epsilon — is just writing down the Prover's response and verifying it works.

**Why the definition is structured the way it is:**

- **"For all epsilon > 0"**: the Skeptic chooses ANY precision requirement
- **"there exists delta > 0"**: the Prover finds a corresponding input neighborhood
- **"such that |x - a| < delta implies |f(x) - L| < epsilon"**: inputs in the delta-neighborhood produce outputs in the epsilon-neighborhood

The order matters critically. "For all epsilon, there exists delta" (limit exists) is different from "there exists delta, for all epsilon" (which would mean one fixed delta works for ALL precisions — that's almost never true and much stronger than what limits require).

Epsilon is the **output tolerance** — how close to L must f(x) be? Delta is the **input tolerance** — how close to a must x be to guarantee the output tolerance? The limit exists when you can always trade a sufficiently tight input tolerance for any desired output tolerance.

What is the CAP theorem in plain English?

<think>
The user is asking for a plain English explanation of the CAP theorem, which means I should avoid formal proofs and focus on intuition. The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems, the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition. I should frame it as a concrete decision: when servers can't talk to each other, do you refuse to serve requests (choosing consistency) or serve potentially stale data (choosing availability)? Real-world examples make this concrete: banking systems must choose consistency for financial transactions, social media feeds can choose availability because slightly stale content is acceptable. The important practical nuance is that most real systems don't make a binary choice — they choose different tradeoffs for different operations within the same system. I want to keep this accessible since the user explicitly asked for "plain English" and the system prompt says to explain at the right level for the question.
</think>

When a network partition occurs in a distributed system (some servers can't talk to each other), you have to choose:

**Option A: Consistency.** All servers refuse to serve data they might be uncertain about. Users may get errors, but they never get stale or conflicting data. Example: a banking system that temporarily rejects transactions rather than risk double-spending.

**Option B: Availability.** All servers continue serving requests, but some may return stale data because they can't confirm what the latest state is. Example: a social media feed that shows slightly old content rather than going offline.

You can't have both during a partition. When the network heals, consistency is restored.

In practice, most systems choose availability for most operations (users hate errors more than slightly stale data) and consistency for critical operations (you absolutely need consistency for financial transactions).

5. **Permissions on the log file** — `/var/log/sync.log` is writable only by root. If cron is user me, the redirect fails before the script even runs, and the user sees nothing.

Since the symptom is "nothing in the log file", #5 is a real candidate — the redirect failing means script may be running but output never lands. But more often it's PATH or %.

I should give them a triage checklist and the corrected entry, plus tell them how to actually see what cron is doing (`grep CRON /var/log/syslog` or journalctl).
</think>

This is the cron tax. There are four classic causes and you're almost certainly hitting one of them. Diagnose in this order:

**1. Did cron even run the job?**

```bash
# systemd-based
journalctl -u cron --since "30 min ago" | grep sync.sh
# or for the user
grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep sync.sh | tail
```

You should see lines like `CRON[12345]: (me) CMD (/home/me/scripts/sync.sh ...)`. If you don't, cron isn't picking up your crontab — usually a syntax error (run `crontab -l` to confirm it's actually installed) or you edited the wrong user's crontab.

**2. Can the redirect actually write to the log?**

`/var/log/sync.log` is in `/var/log/`, which is owned by root. As an unprivileged user, your shell redirect fails before the script's first line runs. **You see nothing because there's nothing to see — the shell errored out trying to open the log.** Move the log somewhere your user owns:

```cron
*/5 * * * * /home/me/scripts/sync.sh > /home/me/log/sync.log 2>&1
```

Or `sudo touch /var/log/sync.log && sudo chown me /var/log/sync.log`.

**3. PATH.** Cron's default PATH is usually `/usr/bin:/bin`. If your script calls `aws`, `python3` (from a pyenv/venv), `kubectl`, `docker`, `node`, `psql`, anything in `/usr/local/bin`, `~/bin`, `~/.cargo/bin`, etc. — it won't be found. Fix at the top of the crontab:

```cron
SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/home/me/bin
MAILTO=me@example.com

*/5 * * * * /home/me/scripts/sync.sh > /home/me/log/sync.log 2>&1
```

`MAILTO` is critical: any stderr that escapes your redirect goes to local mail by default (`/var/mail/me`) which you've probably never read. Setting MAILTO to a real address — or to empty string `MAILTO=""` to discard — makes failure visible.

**4. The `%` trap.** In a crontab entry, `%` characters are converted to newlines, and everything after the first unescaped `%` becomes stdin to the command. So this:

```cron
0 2 * * * /usr/bin/pg_dump -f /backup/db-$(date +%Y%m%d).sql
```

breaks. cron sees the command as `... -f /backup/db-$(date +`, and `Y%m%d).sql` becomes stdin. Escape with backslash:

```cron
0 2 * * * /usr/bin/pg_dump -f /backup/db-$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).sql
```

Or — better — put the logic in the script and keep the crontab entry simple.

**Diagnostic trick:** to see what cron *actually* sees as your environment, add a one-time job:

```cron
* * * * * env > /tmp/cron-env.txt; exit
```

Wait a minute, then `cat /tmp/cron-env.txt`. Compare to your shell's `env`. The diff is exactly what bites you.

**The robust pattern** is to make the script not depend on the calling environment. At the top of `sync.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
export PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
cd "$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
exec >> /home/me/log/sync.log 2>&1
echo "=== run $(date -Is) ==="
# ... actual work
```

That way the crontab entry can just be `*/5 * * * * /home/me/scripts/sync.sh` and your script controls its own destiny — including its own log file, which sidesteps the permission issue entirely.

That said, the most common fix for your shape of workload is a **multicolumn GiST index** combining geometry and timestamp:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

CREATE INDEX gps_points_geom_ts_idx
  ON gps_points
  USING GIST (geom, timestamp);
```

The `btree_gist` extension teaches GiST how to index scalar types like timestamp inside the same R-tree structure as your geometry. The index entries become 3D bounding boxes (lon, lat, time), and a query with `ST_Within(geom, $polygon) AND timestamp BETWEEN $t1 AND $t2` prunes both dimensions in a single descent. Two single-column indexes force Postgres to build two bitmaps and AND them — at your scale that AND is doing a lot of pointless work.

- Build it `CONCURRENTLY` on a 120M-row table or you'll lock writes for hours.
- It's larger than a pure-geom GiST. Budget ~1.5x the size of your current GiST.
- The column order in GiST doesn't matter the way it does in btree, but list the more selective column first as a habit.

BRIN on geom does exist via `brin_inclusion_ops` and it's tiny — typically <0.1% the size of an equivalent GiST. The problem is that BRIN summarizes contiguous page ranges with a bounding box, and it's only useful if rows on the same page are spatially close.

GPS point data is almost always inserted in roughly time order, with devices interleaved. So the rows on physical page 50,000 might be: device_A in Brooklyn, device_B in Los Angeles, device_C in Berlin, device_A in Manhattan. The BRIN summary for that range becomes a bounding box covering most of the planet, and a polygon query in Brooklyn matches every range. You read the same number of pages as a seq scan, plus the recheck overhead.

You can verify whether this is your situation:

```sql
SELECT correlation
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'gps_points' AND attname = 'geom';
```

Geom doesn't have a meaningful scalar correlation, so the trick is to compute it on a space-filling curve:

```sql
SELECT corr(row_number, geohash_int)
FROM (
  SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ctid) AS row_number,
         ST_GeoHash(geom, 6)::bit(30)::bigint AS geohash_int
  FROM gps_points TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1)
) s;
```

If that correlation is below ~0.7, BRIN on geom is a trap.

**To make it work**, you'd need to physically reorder the table by a space-filling curve. The two real options:

```sql
-- Option A: rebuild the table sorted by geohash + time
CREATE TABLE gps_points_new (LIKE gps_points INCLUDING ALL);
INSERT INTO gps_points_new
SELECT * FROM gps_points
ORDER BY ST_GeoHash(geom, 7), timestamp;

-- Option B: CLUSTER on a btree of geohash (locks the table)
CREATE INDEX gps_points_geohash ON gps_points (ST_GeoHash(geom, 7));
CLUSTER gps_points USING gps_points_geohash;
```

After that, BRIN on geom with `pages_per_range = 32` (smaller than default 128 for tighter summaries) is excellent and a BRIN on timestamp essentially comes for free.

For your existing 120M-row table I'd start with the multicolumn GiST. It's a one-shot `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and you keep the table layout. Reserve the BRIN+space-filling-curve approach for the next major rebuild — for example, when you partition by month, sort each new partition by H3 cell during ingest. New data goes into a layout that BRIN can exploit, old data lives on GiST, and you migrate gradually.

- SP-GiST is a partition tree (quad-tree or k-d tree for spatial): non-overlapping space partition, depth varies. Faster for point-in-region queries on uniformly distributed points, sometimes 2-3x. Worse for skewed data and worse for variable-size geometries.

The practical wins:
1. Pure point data with reasonably uniform distribution — SP-GiST quad-tree often beats GiST for `ST_Contains(polygon, point)` queries.
2. Smaller index size for points (no overlapping boxes to store).
3. K-NN queries (`ORDER BY geom <-> ref_point`) work well with SP-GiST quad/k-d trees.

Where it loses:
1. Mixed geometry types or polygons — GiST is better.
2. Skewed distributions (most points in cities, few in oceans) — SP-GiST trees become unbalanced and pathological.
3. Workloads with lots of inserts — SP-GiST insert cost can be higher and there's no easy concurrent build until recent versions.
4. No support for 3D bounding box queries the way GiST has with btree_gist.

SP-GiST wins in a narrower set of cases than the docs sometimes suggest. The mental model:

- **GiST** is an R-tree. Each node stores a bounding box that may overlap siblings. Insert cost is moderate, lookup descends multiple subtrees when boxes overlap. Robust across all geometry types.
- **SP-GiST** is a space-partitioning tree — for PostGIS that's a quad-tree (`spgist_quad_ops`) or k-d tree on point data. Partitions don't overlap. Lookup descends exactly one branch per level. Smaller, sometimes faster, but only when the partition is well-balanced.

The wins fall into three buckets:

**1. Pure-point tables with roughly uniform distribution.** Think IoT sensor readings spread across a region, or astronomical catalogs. The quad-tree partitions evenly, and `ST_Contains(polygon, point)` lookups become O(log n) descents with no overlap-induced backtracking. I've seen 2-3x improvements over GiST in this exact scenario.

```sql
CREATE INDEX sensors_geom_idx
  ON sensors
  USING SPGIST (geom);
```

**2. K-nearest-neighbor on points.** `ORDER BY geom <-> ST_MakePoint(...)` LIMIT 10 against an SP-GiST quad-tree is genuinely fast because the tree gives you a clean ordering by partition distance. GiST handles this too but does more work pruning overlapping boxes.

**3. Index size matters.** SP-GiST stores no bounding boxes for the points themselves, just the partition prefixes. For a billion points the size difference is meaningful.

Where SP-GiST loses for your workload:

- **Skewed distribution.** GPS points cluster heavily in cities. A quad-tree on skewed data goes deep on the dense partitions and the per-lookup descent cost grows. GiST's R-tree adapts to density better because it splits by data, not by space.
- **Mixed or non-point geometries.** SP-GiST has no good polygon support in PostGIS. If your column is `GEOMETRY` (not `POINT`) and you might insert a polygon someday, it's GiST.
- **Multicolumn with timestamp.** SP-GiST doesn't compose with `btree_gist`. You can't build the spatiotemporal index we discussed earlier.
- **Frequent inserts with index growth.** SP-GiST split logic is more rigid; GiST is more graceful under churn.

For your 120M GPS points, stay with the multicolumn GiST. With a gateway, the contract is a typed interface:

```python
from typing import Protocol
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ChargeResult:
    id: str
    status: str  # 'succeeded' | 'failed' | 'pending'
    failure_code: str | None = None

class StripeGateway(Protocol):
    def create_charge(self, amount_cents: int, customer: str,
                      idempotency_key: str) -> ChargeResult: ...
```

Now you have two implementations:

```python
class FakeStripeGateway:
    def __init__(self):
        self._queue: list[ChargeResult] = []
        self.calls: list[dict] = []
    def queue(self, result: ChargeResult) -> None:
        self._queue.append(result)
    def create_charge(self, amount_cents, customer, idempotency_key):
        self.calls.append({'amount_cents': amount_cents, 'customer': customer,
                           'idempotency_key': idempotency_key})
        return self._queue.pop(0)

class LiveStripeGateway:
    def __init__(self, api_key: str):
        self._client = stripe.Client(api_key=api_key)
    def create_charge(self, amount_cents, customer, idempotency_key):
        raw = self._client.charges.create(
            amount=amount_cents, customer=customer,
            idempotency_key=idempotency_key,
        )
        return ChargeResult(id=raw.id, status=raw.status,
                            failure_code=raw.get('failure_code'))
```

```python
import ast, sys, pathlib

INTERNAL_PACKAGES = ('payments.', 'auth.', 'billing.')

def check(path: pathlib.Path) -> list[str]:
    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text())
    issues = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if (isinstance(node, ast.Call)
                and isinstance(node.func, ast.Attribute)
                and node.func.attr == 'patch'
                and node.args
                and isinstance(node.args[0], ast.Constant)
                and any(node.args[0].value.startswith(p) for p in INTERNAL_PACKAGES)):
            issues.append(f'{path}:{node.lineno}: mocker.patch on internal module')
    return issues
```

### Month 2-6: opportunistic migration

Two rules:

1. **Boy scout rule**: when you touch a test file for any reason, port one test to the new pattern. Not all of them — one. Keep the PR scoped to your actual change.

2. **Regression-first rule**: every production bug that tests missed gets an integration test *before* the fix ships. This is where migration has the highest ROI — you have a concrete failure mode and the new-style test proves you solved it. Do not write a new-style test that passes without first showing it fails on the unfixed code.

Don't track 'migration percentage.' That's a vanity metric and it incentivizes shallow rewrites. Track 'production bugs caught by tests in staging' — that's what you actually care about.

- Don't delete old tests before replacing their coverage. They're bad but they're not zero — they at least exercise the code path. Leave them until new coverage exists.
- Don't make migration a quarterly OKR. It becomes performative. Make bug-catching the OKR and let migration happen organically.

How do I write efficient SQL queries?

<think>
The user wants to write efficient SQL queries. This is a practical data engineering question where I should focus on the most impactful optimizations rather than trying to be comprehensive. I'll organize by descending impact.

First, SELECT * is the most common performance mistake — fetching unnecessary columns wastes I/O, memory, and prevents covering index usage. Second, index design is critical — I should show a composite index example that matches the query's WHERE and ORDER BY clauses, since many developers create indexes on single columns without understanding column order matters.

N+1 queries are an application-level problem that devastates performance — a JOIN replacing N individual queries is often a 10-100x improvement. EXISTS vs IN for correlated subqueries is a classic optimization that leverages short-circuit evaluation. Cursor-based pagination vs OFFSET is important for any application with large datasets — OFFSET must scan and discard rows, while cursor-based pagination uses the index directly.

I'll end with EXPLAIN ANALYZE as the meta-advice: always measure before optimizing, because the actual bottleneck is rarely where developers assume it is. This reinforces evidence-based engineering over cargo-cult optimization.
</think>

**1. Select only what you need:**
```sql
-- Bad: fetches all columns
SELECT * FROM orders;

-- Good: only what you use
SELECT id, user_id, total, status FROM orders;
```

**2. Use indexes effectively:**
```sql
-- This query benefits from an index on (user_id, status)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status, created_at DESC);
```

**3. Avoid N+1 queries:**
```sql
-- Bad: one query per user to get their orders
-- Good: one query with a join
SELECT u.name, o.id, o.total
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.active = true;
```

**4. Use EXISTS instead of IN for subqueries:**
```sql
-- Slower (evaluates full subquery)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);

-- Faster (stops at first match per row)
SELECT * FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
);
```

**5. Paginate with cursors, not OFFSET:**
```sql
-- Bad: OFFSET 10000 scans and discards 10000 rows
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000;

-- Good: cursor-based (uses index)
SELECT * FROM items WHERE id > 10000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;
```

**6. Always EXPLAIN ANALYZE** before optimizing. The bottleneck is rarely where you think.

The advice to 'just use StatefulSet' is half right. Let me break down what it actually does, then tell you when it's insufficient.

**Deployment vs StatefulSet, concretely.**

| Behavior | Deployment | StatefulSet |
|--|--|--|
| Pod names | `app-7d4b9c8f5-xk2pq` (random hash) | `app-0`, `app-1`, `app-2` (ordinal) |
| Pod identity across restarts | New random name each time | Same name, same DNS |
| Storage | Shared or none (from spec.volumes) | Per-pod PVC from `volumeClaimTemplates` |
| Rollout order | Parallel by default (maxSurge/maxUnavailable) | Strictly ordered: N-1 down, updated, back up, then N-2 |
| Scale-up order | Parallel | One at a time: 0, then 1, then 2 |
| Scale-down order | Random | Reverse ordinal: N-1, then N-2 |
| Requires | A Service | A **headless** Service |

**The headless service is load-bearing.** A headless service (`clusterIP: None`) doesn't assign a virtual IP — instead, DNS returns the individual pod IPs. Combined with StatefulSet's stable hostnames, every replica gets a predictable, persistent DNS name:

```
postgres-0.postgres-headless.databases.svc.cluster.local
postgres-1.postgres-headless.databases.svc.cluster.local
postgres-2.postgres-headless.databases.svc.cluster.local
```

This matters because stateful systems need to reason about peers. A Postgres replica needs to know it's replicating *from* `postgres-0`, specifically, not from 'whatever pod the load balancer picks.'

**Minimal working manifest.**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres-headless
  namespace: databases
spec:
  clusterIP: None            # headless
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
    - port: 5432
      name: postgres
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: databases
spec:
  serviceName: postgres-headless   # MUST match the headless Service
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        storageClassName: gp3-retain
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi
```

`volumeClaimTemplates` is the magic. Each pod gets its own PVC — `data-postgres-0`, `data-postgres-1`, `data-postgres-2` — bound to its own PV, reattached on every restart, surviving pod deletion.

**PVC lifecycle gotcha.** Deleting the StatefulSet does NOT delete the PVCs. That's usually what you want (data survives), but it catches people:

```
kubectl delete sts postgres -n databases
kubectl get pvc -n databases
NAME               STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY
data-postgres-0    Bound    pvc-8a7c1f92-...                           100Gi
data-postgres-1    Bound    pvc-2d4e7a31-...                           100Gi
data-postgres-2    Bound    pvc-9b1c3d55-...                           100Gi
```

Recreate the StatefulSet with the same name and the new `postgres-0` pod binds to the old `data-postgres-0` PVC — data restored. To actually delete storage, remove the PVCs explicitly. Since 1.27, you can set `.spec.persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` to auto-delete on scale-down or sts-delete:

```yaml
spec:
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain      # or Delete
    whenScaled: Retain       # or Delete
```

**Ordered rollout, and why it sometimes bites.** Updating a StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady` (default) takes down `postgres-2`, waits until it's Ready again, then `postgres-1`, then `postgres-0`. Safe, but slow — 3 replicas × 60s startup = ~3 minutes of partial capacity. For stateless-ish workloads that only need stable identity (not ordered startup), set `podManagementPolicy: Parallel`.

**Now — the real question. Should you even use raw StatefulSet for Postgres?**

Probably not. StatefulSet gives you the plumbing — stable names, stable storage, ordered ops — but it has no idea what Postgres *is*. It doesn't know:

- Which replica is the primary (writable) vs the followers (read-only)
- How to promote a follower when the primary's node dies
- How to bootstrap a new replica (`pg_basebackup` against the current primary)
- How to schedule, store, and restore base backups + WAL
- How to perform minor version upgrades without data loss
- How to do point-in-time recovery

Those are all your problem with raw StatefulSet. That's what Operators solve. For Postgres specifically, **CloudNativePG** (CNCF graduated) is the current best-in-class option. You write a Cluster CRD, it generates the StatefulSet underneath plus failover logic, backup CronJobs, and a managed primary-service that always routes to the current writer:

```yaml
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: databases
spec:
  instances: 3
  storage:
    size: 100Gi
    storageClass: gp3-retain
  backup:
    barmanObjectStore:
      destinationPath: s3://my-backups/postgres
      s3Credentials:
        accessKeyId:
          name: s3-creds
          key: ACCESS_KEY_ID
        secretAccessKey:
          name: s3-creds
          key: SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
    retentionPolicy: 30d
```

Rough decision rule:

- **Raw StatefulSet is right** for: single-instance databases where the blast radius is small, queue workers needing stable identity, in-house systems that already know how to cluster themselves (e.g. Elasticsearch in some configurations).
- **Operator is right** for: anything with leader/follower semantics, replication, or multi-step operational workflows. Postgres (CloudNativePG or Zalando), MySQL (Percona, Oracle), Kafka (Strimzi), Redis (Redis Operator), etcd (etcd-operator).

If you're deploying a 3-replica Postgres cluster for real production traffic, install CloudNativePG. If you're standing up a dev Postgres for a demo, a bare StatefulSet is fine.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses separate models for reading and writing data. The write model is optimized for consistency and business logic; the read model is optimized for query performance.

**The simplest form:**
```python
# Write side: normalized, consistent
class OrderService:
    async def create_order(self, cmd: CreateOrderCommand):
        order = Order(customer_id=cmd.customer_id)
        for item in cmd.items:
            order.add_item(item)  # Business rules enforced
        await self.repo.save(order)
        await self.event_bus.publish(OrderCreated(order))

# Read side: denormalized, fast
class OrderReadModel:
    async def get_order_summary(self, order_id: str):
        # Single query against a denormalized table
        return await self.db.fetchone("""
            SELECT order_id, customer_name, item_count,
                   total_amount, status, created_at
            FROM order_summaries WHERE order_id = $1
        """, order_id)

# Projection: keeps read model in sync
@event_handler(OrderCreated)
async def update_read_model(event: OrderCreated):
    await db.execute("""
        INSERT INTO order_summaries
        (order_id, customer_name, item_count, total_amount, status, created_at)
        VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6)
    """, ...)
```

**When CQRS makes sense:**
- Read and write patterns are very different (complex writes, simple reads or vice versa)
- Read-heavy systems where query optimization is critical
- Systems that need different scaling for reads vs writes
- When combined with Event Sourcing (the event log IS the write model)

**When CQRS is overkill:**

Your professor is right, and the concrete thing that breaks has a name: **condition number squaring**. Let me show you exactly how it bites.

**The setup.** Least squares: find x minimizing ||A x - b||_2. The normal equations approach solves

    A^T A x = A^T b

by forming the Gram matrix A^T A (which is square and, if A has full column rank, positive definite), then solving via Cholesky or LU. The QR approach factors A = Q R with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular, then solves

    R x = Q^T b

by back-substitution. Mathematically, in exact arithmetic, both produce the same x. Numerically, they diverge — badly.

**The condition number issue.** The condition number kappa(A) measures how much solving A x = b amplifies input errors. For least squares with matrix A, the relevant condition number is kappa(A) = sigma_max(A) / sigma_min(A) (ratio of largest to smallest singular value).

Here's the killer fact: kappa(A^T A) = kappa(A)^2.

Why? The singular values of A^T A are the squares of the singular values of A. So the ratio squares too. If A is moderately ill-conditioned with kappa(A) = 10^6, then kappa(A^T A) = 10^{12}. Double-precision floating point gives you about 16 digits of precision; you just burned 12 of them forming the Gram matrix.

**A concrete example where normal equations die.** Consider the Lauchli matrix,

    A = [[1, 1],
         [eps, 0],
         [0, eps]],

for small eps > 0. The columns are slightly tilted apart; A has full column rank.

Form A^T A:

    A^T A = [[1 + eps^2, 1],
             [1,         1 + eps^2]].

Now here's the problem. In double precision, machine epsilon is about 2.2 x 10^-16. If you pick eps = 10^-8, then eps^2 = 10^-16, and when the machine computes 1 + 10^-16 it rounds to exactly 1. So in floating point:

    A^T A = [[1, 1],
             [1, 1]].

That matrix is singular. Cholesky will fail (or produce garbage). Your normal-equations solver blows up on a problem that is, mathematically, perfectly well-posed. The true A has rank 2, and a QR decomposition of A would proceed fine — Householder reflections never compute eps^2, they operate on eps directly.

Run this experiment in NumPy:

```python
import numpy as np
eps = 1e-8
A = np.array([[1, 1], [eps, 0], [0, eps]])
b = np.array([2.0, eps, eps])

# Normal equations
AtA = A.T @ A
Atb = A.T @ b
x_normal = np.linalg.solve(AtA, Atb)

# QR
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)
x_qr = np.linalg.solve(R, Q.T @ b)

print(x_normal, x_qr)
```

At eps = 10^-8, normal equations give a visibly wrong answer; QR gives [1, 1] to full precision. Push eps a little smaller and normal equations fail outright.

**Why your test data hasn't shown this.** You're probably fitting well-conditioned problems. If A has kappa(A) = 10 or 100, squaring it to 100 or 10000 is still far below machine precision, so normal equations work fine and are even a bit faster. The problem is that in real-world data — polynomial fits of degree 10+, design matrices with correlated features, anything approaching rank deficiency — the condition number climbs fast. Once kappa(A) exceeds 10^8, normal equations start lying to you. And you don't always know kappa(A) in advance.

**The rule of thumb.** QR (or SVD for extra safety) has backward error O(machine_eps * kappa(A)). Normal equations have forward error O(machine_eps * kappa(A)^2). For benign problems both are fine; for anything borderline, normal equations throw away precision you can't afford.

Extra detail worth knowing: scikit-learn, LAPACK's `gelsy`/`gels`, MATLAB's backslash for tall matrices, and essentially every production library use QR or SVD by default, *not* normal equations. The speed advantage of normal equations (roughly 2x fewer flops) is almost never worth the stability cost on real problems.

Keep normal equations in your toolkit for the well-conditioned case, but ship QR. Your future self debugging a polynomial fit at degree 12 will thank you.

Let me start with the simplest possible demonstration.

**Multiplying by i is rotation by 90 degrees.**

Plot 1 on the complex plane — it's at position (1, 0), pointing right along the real axis. Now multiply by i:

- i * i = i^2 = -1 → position (-1, 0), pointing left
- -1 * i = -i → position (0, -1), pointing down
- -i * i = -i^2 = 1 → back to (1, 0)

Four multiplications by i rotate through 90, 180, 270, 360 degrees and return to the start. That's not a coincidence or a trick — it IS what i does. The number i is a **90-degree rotation operator**.

**The general case: multiplication = rotation + scaling**

Write any complex number in polar form: z = r * e^(i*theta), where r is the distance from the origin and theta is the angle from the positive real axis.

Now multiply two complex numbers:
z1 * z2 = (r1 * e^(i*theta1)) * (r2 * e^(i*theta2)) = r1*r2 * e^(i*(theta1 + theta2))

The distances multiply (scaling). The angles add (rotation). Every multiplication by a complex number is a **rotation by its angle and a scaling by its magnitude**.

**A concrete example**

Multiply 3 + 4i by 1 + i.

Algebraically: (3+4i)(1+i) = 3 + 3i + 4i + 4i^2 = 3 + 7i - 4 = -1 + 7i.

Geometrically: 3+4i has magnitude 5 and angle arctan(4/3) ≈ 53.1 degrees. 1+i has magnitude sqrt(2) and angle 45 degrees. The product should have magnitude 5*sqrt(2) ≈ 7.07 and angle 53.1 + 45 = 98.1 degrees. Check: |-1+7i| = sqrt(1+49) = sqrt(50) = 5*sqrt(2). Angle of (-1, 7): arctan(7/-1) in the second quadrant ≈ 98.1 degrees. It works perfectly.

**Why this matters for circuits**

An AC voltage V(t) = V_0 * cos(omega*t) is the real part of V_0 * e^(i*omega*t). That exponential is a point rotating around the origin at angular velocity omega. The phasor V_0 * e^(i*phi) captures the amplitude and phase in one complex number.

When current flows through an impedance Z = R + iX, the voltage is V = I * Z. This multiplication rotates the current phasor by the impedance's angle (the phase shift) and scales it by the impedance's magnitude. A purely resistive load (Z = R, angle 0) doesn't shift the phase. A purely inductive load (Z = i*omega*L, angle 90 degrees) shifts current by 90 degrees — which is why inductors cause current to lag voltage by a quarter cycle. The complex number isn't a trick; it IS the rotation.

**The three series you know**

e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + x^4/4! + x^5/5! + ...

cos(x) = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - x^6/6! + ...

Compute the powers of i: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, i^5 = i, ... (cycles every 4)

= 1 + i*theta - theta^2/2! - i*theta^3/3! + theta^4/4! + i*theta^5/5! - ...

Now separate real and imaginary parts:

Real: 1 - theta^2/2! + theta^4/4! - ... = **cos(theta)**

Imaginary: theta - theta^3/3! + theta^5/5! - ... = **sin(theta)**

Therefore: e^(i*theta) = cos(theta) + i*sin(theta).

The exponential, cosine, and sine are secretly the same function, just viewed from different angles. When you feed i*theta into the exponential, the alternating powers of i sort the terms into exactly the cosine series (real part) and the sine series (imaginary part).

This also tells you that e^(i*theta) traces the unit circle. Its real part is cos(theta) and its imaginary part is sin(theta), so it's at position (cos(theta), sin(theta)) — which is exactly the point on the unit circle at angle theta. As theta increases, the point rotates counterclockwise. At theta = pi: e^(i*pi) = cos(pi) + i*sin(pi) = -1 + 0i = -1, which gives you Euler's identity: e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0.

**A differential equations perspective (bonus)**
